speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Coming as I do from the silver city of Canada, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance if he has decided upon any way of commemorating the centennial of British Columbia. There have been several requests to have the department strike a silver dollar before the celebration in 1958. Has the minister come to any decision on that matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR COMMEMORATIVE DOLLAR ON OCCASION OF CENTENARY CELEBRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member's question may I say the government has decided to issue a coin to commemorate the one hundredth anniversary of the gold rush and the creation of British Columbia as a crown colony in 1858.
In order to do so we have decided to hold a competition of Canadian artists and sculptors for a design for a commemorative silver dollar. A committee under the chairmanship of Mr. A. P. Williams, master of the Royal Canadian Mint, will judge the entries. A prize of $1,000 will be given to the artist who submits the design that is accepted and four additional prizes of $250 each may be given for those receiving honourable mention. The competition will close on December 31, 1956.

Mr. Speaker, may I preface the question I am about to ask by extending to the Prime Minister every good wish on the occasion of his trip to the commonwealth prime ministers' conference in London. That comes from everyone in the house. My question is this. First, would the Prime Minister be prepared to outline in general some of the views that he intends to express on the agenda to which reference is made in today's papers? Second, what stand does he intend to take with reference to the question of extending the British preference, which apparently is one of the basic considerations to come before the conference, as a means whereby trade within the commonwealth and also among the free nations will be expanded and extended in order to meet the U.S.S.R. world trade offensive?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member and all hon. members of the house for their good wishes, and I hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and I will be able to do our share in producing fruitful results from the conference in London. I do not think it would be proper for me to state what views we will support. They will be subject to the discussions that will take place in respect to each matter that comes before the conference.
With respect to the extension of the British preference, if that is discussed in the plenary meeting my colleague and I will be very interested to hear the views expressed by other members of the commonwealth in that regard. The hon. gentleman may be assured that we are still firmly convinced that dollars earned in the Canadian market through the sale in the Canadian market of exports from commonwealth countries do increase the volume of Canadian commodities that it is


possible for us to sell in those markets, and that we are very anxious, as I am sure all hon. members are, to have as much world trade promoted through the efforts of the commonwealth as it is possible to achieve.
The situation is a complex one and one that will, if discussed there, have to be considered in all its aspects. I can assure the house that we will do everything possible that would tend to increase the volume of exchanges between commonwealth countries.

Various members of the British press have reported that the Canadian government, and in particular the Prime Minister, would be opposed to any extension of the British preference. Would the Prime Minister say whether or not that is correct?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is not correct as a general statement. The matter will have to be considered in all its aspects and of course in the light of its possible repercussions upon the general tariff and trade arrangements which are still in force and which have proved to be of quite substantial benefit to Canadian trade.

That a sum not exceeding $264,409,639.92 being one-twelfth of the total of the amounts of the items set forth in the main estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1957, laid before the House of Commons at the present session of parliament; and a sum not exceeding $12,168,792.75, being one-twelfth of the total of the amounts of items set forth in the supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1957, be granted to Her Majesty on account of the fiscal year ending March 31, 1957.
He said: Mr. Chairman, as the resolution indicates, the proposed bill to be founded on the resolution will provide for one-twelfth

of all the items to be voted in the main estimates for the fiscal year 1956-57 and one-twelfth of all the items in the supplementary estimates for the same fiscal year. This bill is to provide for all necessary ordinary requirements to the end of July. No additional proportions are being provided for at this time. In no instance is the total amount of any item being requested.
The passing of this bill-if it is passed- will not prejudice the rights and privileges of members to criticize and discuss any item in the estimates which will come up for consideration from time to time through the balance of the session, and the usual undertaking is hereby given that such rights and privileges will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as a result of the passing of this measure.

Mr. Chairman, this motion to
provide interim supply for the month of July follows very shortly after a similar motion to cover interim supply for the month of June. I think I should explain the position that we take with regard to interim supply. It is difficult to realize that it was only at the beginning of last week that we were dealing with this subject for the whole of the present month. Interim supply would have a different meaning if we were not sitting continuously to deal with estimates.
I want to make one thing clear. When two weeks ago today I asked the Prime Minister whether it was the intention of the government to adjourn for the summer months or to proceed with a continuous session, I was directing that question to the possibility that the government was asking for only a month's interim supply and might then adjourn, as had been indicated generally in the press, without having provided for the period during which the house would not be sitting. I also had in mind that, if this was done, the only course the government could follow in paying the civil servants, the members of the armed forces and, in fact, all the many people dependent upon payments month by month from the government, would be to resort to governor general's warrants.
From the nature of my questions both on Friday two weeks ago and a week ago Monday I think it must be clear that if there had not been a continuous examination of the estimates and if there had been any attempt to adjourn with only a month's supply voted, we would not have consented to the voting of supply.
However, I want to remind the members of the house that interim supply does not in any way prejudice the consideration of the estimates, as has already been undertaken by the Minister of Finance. We are simply
Interim Supply
asked to provide for one-twelfth of the total amount that is estimated as the requirement of the government. The granting of this amount permits payment of the necessary monthly payments of every kind, without prejudice to the details of any item in the estimates. We are continuing to discuss those estimates and, therefore, we follow the practice that has been followed on other occasions, without exception, in the past. There has, in fact, been no case in Canadian history where there was a protracted debate in regard to the ordinary voting of one month's supply. There was a case in 1921 when there was objection to the voting of two month's supply. In fact, on that occasion there was vigorous opposition to that procedure.
But it has been the invariable practice to permit the payments that are required to carry out the ordinary business of the people of Canada. It is not the business of the government. It is not the prerogative of the government. It is the rights of the people of Canada who are dealing with the Canadian government, whatever that government may be, to have the payments they expect on time. Under those circumstances, and in view of the fact that we are continuing to deal with the estimates, it is not our purpose to seek to prevent the ordinary payments being made. May I leave no doubt that had we thought it was possible to force an election by delay on the earlier occasion, we would certainly have followed that course. The government, however, had made it quite clear it had no intention at that time of acceding to our proposal. We took the position, and take the position again, that while we have no confidence in the attitude of this government toward parliament, while we believe this government has no moral right to govern in view of its conduct, nevertheless we do not believe the civil servants, members of the armed forces and people doing business with the government should become the victims of any procedure that might be adopted as the result of the actions of the government itself. That is what the result would be.
While it is not our intention to delay the voting of interim supply, nevertheless it is my intention to avail myself of the appropriate opportunity to discuss certain subjects which are related to the broad details of the motion before us. As will be realized by every hon. member in this house, any item included in the estimates can be discussed. I do intend to discuss one or two subjects which could very properly be embraced in the remarks that are made in relation to a motion of this nature. One thing about which I want to speak is the speech made by the Minister of Finance a week ago tonight over the trans-Canada network of the C.B.C. It

House of Commons
is a mass of inaccuracies, but those inaccuracies can be dealt with on other occasions.
I am going to deal with one statement that was made by the Minister of Finance and I do so because if there is one minister in this house who should not have made that statement it is the Minister of Finance. I am going to quote from the printed copy of the speech which was issued by the National Liberal Federation of Canada. These are the words contained in that speech which I assume were the words used over the radio:
I am not going to say very much about the action taken by the Leader of the Opposition, Mr. George Drew, in attacking the Deputy Speaker and in moving in parliament that the house no longer had confidence in its Speaker. No one who understands our British parliamentary system would question the right of the opposition or the duty of the opposition, to oppose the government and to introduce motions to embarrass the government and to express lack of confidence in the government. That is the right of an opposition. Indeed, the opposition has a duty to try to defeat the government. But it is one thing to attack the government and a very different thing to attack the presiding officers who represent the authority of parliament itself.
The members of the opposition who supported Mr. Drew in attacking the Speaker admitted that before the pipe line debate began, he had been a good Speaker; some of them said the best Speaker the Canadian parliament had ever had. Yet, they felt they were justified in attacking a respected officer of parliament and seeking to destroy his reputation.
I cannot believe the people of Canada will easily forget or easily forgive conduct of that kind, conduct which, if persisted in, would destroy the institution of parliament itself.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, the applause which has come from hon. members opposite including the man who has been directing the affairs of the government, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, indicates very clearly why this government has no moral right to govern. The very fact they applaud a statement of this kind indicates how little consciousness there is of what this government has done to destroy the institution of parliament in Canada. The man who accepted the primary responsibility of a course of that kind was the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has applauded that statement. It was he who, in spite of the statement of the minister that the opposition had the right to oppose the government, denied that normal right by moving closure before there had been a word said in this house by any member of the opposition; and it was the Minister of Finance who was mainly responsible for the circumstances which led to the motions relating to the Deputy Speaker and the Speaker which were presented to this house.

It is the Prime Minister who, as head of the government, must accept the full moral responsibility for the abomination which occurred here during the course of the debate which closed just two weeks ago.

Here is the man who is mainly responsible for making the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker victims of the government's conduct. I would point out it was not an attack made on the Speaker by members of the opposition which brought this subject before parliament; it was the way in which the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker and those responsible for the conduct of business in this house were forced into a position of subservience to the will of the government in pushing through a measure which the government had determined to have passed by this house no matter what took place and no matter what rule was broken.
