And the minister knows perfectly well that the government did violate the rules. He also knows perfectly well the government was a party to the violation of the rules. He knows very well the position we have taken with regard to the Speaker-
This speech is a violation of the rules.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot in this case ignore the interruption by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in which he said that this speech is a violation of the rules. In the mind of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration any statement by the opposition is a violation of the rights of the government. I noticed one statement in the speech of the Minister of Finance that there were two members of the opposition who had spoken 30 times. That total was arrived at by adding up the number of times comments had been made by certain members of the opposition. If the Minister of Finance will examine Hansard and look at the number of times the name of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration appears he will doubtless find by that test that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration spoke more than 100 times during the debate because he was constantly interrupting. I will say this, however; he made those speeches while sitting in his seat and not by taking part in the debate either on the rules or on the subject matter before the house.

One hundred speeches and
nothing said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is a pretty faded rose you are wearing.

I would be very happy to have the hon. member who just interrupted from a reclining position rise and make the statement in the way that statements are supposed to be made before this house. I would be very happy to give him the opportunity to do so. Does the hon. member care to do so or does he wish to remain in a reclining position?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will accept the courtesy and rise and say it is a very faded rose the Leader of the Opposition is wearing this morning.
We still cannot hear you.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad that interruption was put on the record because it indicates the standard of the interruptions which have been made by members supporting this government during the course of the discussion of this whole subject. If the rose I happen to be wearing this morning is faded I would suggest that the hon. member make an appropriate appeal to the correct official of the government because it was cut in my own garden this morning and if it has wilted it is probably only under the impact of remarks such as the hon. member has just made.
He has not even bloomed yet.

Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that the remark that has just been made is
House of Commons
indicative of the type of interruption that has been occurring in this house not only now but during the course of the debate to which I refer.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in view of the statement made by the Minister of Finance, who apparently disagrees with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, because he says the opposition has the right to speak-
I never said the contrary either.

I just want to recall exactly what did take place because I wish to leave no uncertainty as to the circumstances under which the motion was first presented which directed the attention of the house to the conduct of the Deputy Speaker and later the motion dealing with the conduct of the Speaker. May I recall those events. On Thursday night, May 31, the Speaker permitted the presentation of a motion arising on a question of privilege which was in accordance with the rules. The Speaker himself took the initiative in guiding the framing of that motion. The Speaker himself stated that the question was an important question of privilege and he placed the matter before the house for discussion. At that time I rose to speak in the debate on that motion which was properly before the house.
I had spoken for a short time when the house adjourned at ten o'clock. On Friday morning, June 1, the Speaker had not risen when I rose to continue the debate. I was on my feet and the house was seized with the motion, the motion which had been accepted by the Speaker and in fact framed by the Speaker himself because of the advice he had given as to the form it should take. It was under debate and the right to debate had been fully accepted in the house without challenge.
Nevertheless the Speaker then rose and refused to permit me to continue the debate. He refused further to hear me either on the point of order or on the question of privilege. The rules make it clear that he had no right to deny that opportunity to me. He certainly had no right to deny that opportunity when I had already taken the floor and when I was continuing a debate which under his guidance had been before the house the previous evening. He gave no authority of any kind for his position. He denied the motion and to other members the right to discuss the rules. He placed on the records of this house a dangerous precedent which can be quoted in future as a precedent for the taking of an improper course which could destroy the regular procedure in any debate.
House of Commons

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I suggest that the Leader of the Opposition is entirely and completely out of order in attempting to review the actions of Mr. Speaker before you and this committee. I cannot conceive of anything more out of order than to do what he is trying to do. If he is to be permitted to make these statements which are not well-founded, as to what happened and which constitute improper criticism of Mr. Speaker before this committee, then of course he should be answered, but anyone answering him would be also out of order. I submit that he should not be permitted to make these improper statements, which he is making and which are not well-founded either on fact or on the rules, before a committee of this house. He should not be permitted to criticize the conduct of Mr. Speaker and I submit that he is absolutely out of order and should be asked to desist.

Mr. Chairman, every subject which can be dealt with by this parliament can now be properly dealt with on the motion for interim supply. The motion covers one-twelfth of the estimates which embrace every item, including the administration of the Speaker's office. Therefore it is not only appropriate but it is very proper that the discussion should take place at this time in regard to the very inaccurate interpretation given by the Minister of Finance as to what occurred in this house. The remarks which I shall subsequently make will relate themselves very clearly to the position of Speaker and to the estimates of this house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Rosthern has raised a point of order and perhaps I should deal with it following the remarks of the hon. Leader of the Opposition. I have looked at the motion which was moved by the Leader of the Opposition several weeks ago with regard to Mr. Speaker, and I find also that in the estimates there are items dealing with the allowances to Mr. Speaker, to myself and to other officials. Under those circumstances I am unable to find that a discussion of those offices at this time is out of order. However, I do say that it must be a discussion which would be relevant under the items of legislation at a later time; that is the only type of discussion which could take place on a motion for interim supply at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to argue your ruling but I do point out to you that this very point that has been raised by the Leader of the Opposition was raised as a reason for censuring Mr. Speaker and was actually decided on by this house, the only place where it could be decided upon.
IMr. Drew.]
When the house has actually decided upon a question, the question being decided upon being one of the reasons why Mr. Speaker should be censured, when the house decided the question that he should not be censured, I suggest that to permit this to be rehashed before this committee and to ask it to pass judgment on something which has already been decided is out of order entirely.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps I should read the exact terms of the motion, which are as follows:
In view of the unprecedented action of Mr. Speaker in (a) improperly reversing his own decision without notice and without giving any opportunity for discussion; (b) repeatedly refusing to allow members to address the house on occasions when the rules provide that they have the right to be heard; (c) subordinating the rights of the house to the will of the government, this house resolves that it no longer has any confidence in its presiding officer.
I quite agree with the hon. member for Rosthern that matters covered by that motion, which was negatived, cannot be discussed at this time, but I do not see how a discussion of the competence of the Speaker, of myself and others, since these items appear in the estimates and as long as we do not deal with questions which have been decided upon by the house, could be ruled out of order.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to seek a review of a motion which in one case has been ruled to be not debatable, and of a motion which in another case has been voted down. I am dealing with a subject which will come before the house under the estimates and, as Your Honour has indicated, therefore something which it is appropriate to discuss at this time. In doing so I am taking particular issue with certain statements made by the Minister of Finance which have a bearing on this subject. It is my intention simply to state the facts of what occurred because of the relationship with appropriations which will subsequently be dealt with as part of the general estimates of which interim supply will constitute one-twelfth.
Therefore, to continue what I was saying at the time the point of order was raised, I would point out that in making the decision he did on that occasion, without giving any authority whatever for his position, the Speaker has created difficulties in the future for any Speaker who may occupy the chair, because of the precedent which has been established in that way by the actions to which reference has been made. I submit that the Speaker disregarded the following rules or authorities.
Standing order 50 provides that, if it is out of order, the Speaker must so rule before he puts it forward for discussion, and also

that he must give his authority when he rules that a motion is out of order.
Standing order 7 provides that business under consideration at adjournment the night before will be taken up on the next sitting day, "at the same stage where its progress was interrupted."
Standing order 34 (1) provides that a member who has the floor, as I had on the Thursday evening and again on Friday morning two weeks ago, may be interrupted on a point of order, but that after that point has been stated the member may speak to it. I was denied the opportunity to speak to it, and so was every other member of the house.
Standing order No. 17 provides that a point of privilege may be raised at any time. In this case the Speaker refused to hear me on a point of privilege on Friday morning, after he had followed the course he did and while the subject was still under consideration.
Then I would refer to citation 216 of Beauchesne's third edition, which states that the member who moved adjournment of a debate is by courtesy entitled to speak first if he rises in his place when the order for it is called. I had risen before anything had been said and I was therefore entitled to speak under the terms of that citation. Most certainly, if I was not to be allowed to speak, then the explanation should have been given for it.
On Friday morning, June 1, Mr. Speaker did something else without precedent in the annals of this house or of Westminster. He put forward what he described as a proposition to the house, namely that since he had himself made a serious error the previous evening, the house should revert to the position in which it was at the time when he said he had made the error, namely about 5.15 p.m. on Thursday evening. This was something which had no relationship to any course ever followed before. The rules of debate-rules of long antiquity which we have inherited from Westminster-clearly provide that nothing can be submitted to the house for its decision except by way of a motion. That is without qualification.
Recognizing the impropriety of his course of action, Mr. Speaker carefully tried to avoid calling it a motion, because of course the Speaker cannot under the rules initiate a motion before the house. He described his strange procedure as a proposition or course of action which he was submitting to the house for its determination. That in itself was indicative of some unusual circumstances which this house cannot now ignore, any more than it had a right to ignore them then. He did, in fact, as the record will show, fall
House of Commons
into the error on one occasion of calling it a motion when he put the question-an error which he later attempted to correct. However, the brief statement of the position is that nothing can be submitted to the house for its decision by vote unless it is in the form of a motion. Whatever it may be called, therefore, Mr. Speaker actually submitted a motion to the house. In this conduct he was guilty of a breach of the following standing orders or citations:
Standing order 41, which is the general rule providing for 48 hours' notice of a motion before it can be presented to the house for discussion and decision.
Standing order 42, which requires that, generally speaking, if notice is to be waived, unanimous consent for such a course must be obtained.
Standing order 43, which provides that all motions shall be in writing and be seconded before being debated or put from the Chair. This motion was not written or seconded.
Standing order 32 (1) (m), which provides that a motion of this sort, which clearly covers the management of the business of the house, the arrangements of the proceedings of the house, etc., is debatable. The Speaker refused to allow debate.
Citation 135, Beauchesne's third edition, which emphasizes the necessity for strict adherence to the order paper to prevent surprise. A privilege motion was on the order paper and was suddenly removed; the Speaker's proposition was not on the order paper but was suddenly introduced.
Citation 136, Beauchesne's third edition, which provides that all motions referring to the business of the house should be introduced by the leader of the house.
There were specific instances, which have not in any way been wiped from the record by any motion which was dealt with by this house. They have a very direct bearing upon the occupant of the office and the estimates that are provided by that office when the time comes to consider them.

On a point of order again, Mr. Chairman, I think that every member of this house must agree that the action of the Speaker can only be challenged on a specific motion after two days' notice. The Leader of the Opposition is challenging the actions of Mr. Speaker, before a committee of this house, and without any notice. I am not going to refer to the ruling-he can do it-although it has already been decided by the house, but I cite the other ruling. He now is challenging the actions of Mr. Speaker in the house, when the rules lay down both at Westminster and here that

House of Commons
the actions of Mr. Speaker can only be challenged by a specific motion of which notice has been given.
I submit that the Leader of the Opposition has no right to violate the rules on the alleged ground that this vote will affect the salary of Mr. Speaker. In a deliberative assembly such as this and Westminster, when an attempt has been made to call the Speaker into question at a time when a question is involved of voting part of his money, it has been laid down over and over again that he cannot be challenged, nor attacks and derogatory statements made about him, unless a motion is made to that effect, of which 48 hours' notice is given. I submit citation 110 of Beauchesne's second edition:
If a member wishes to challenge the action or conduct of the Speaker on any matter other than an appeal from his decision, he must proceed by giving two days' notice of a motion on the subject and by bringing the matter up as a Separate question, except, of course, if it be a question of privilege when it may be taken up as such.
This is one of the well established rules for protecting the position of the Speaker. The hon. member knows just as well as I do that he is out of order in talking before this committee as he is today.
The chairman says you are out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for Ros-thern raises a question of undoubted difficulty. We have on the one hand a motion which has been negatived by the house. I draw the attention of hon. members to the latter part of standing order 35 which reads:
No member may reflect upon any vote of the house, except for the purpose of moving that such vote be rescinded.
It seems to me that the Leader of the Opposition in his remarks is prevented by the words of the standing order from reflecting on a motion which has been negatived several weeks ago. At the same time, I do not think I can prevent the Leader of the Opposition from discussing the competence of the Speaker or of myself or of any other official who is mentioned in the items which hon. members will find under legislation. I admit quite frankly that it is exceedingly difficult to draw the line but, as long as the Leader of the Opposition does not reflect on the vote which has previously taken place on his own motion, then I believe he is in order. I would take it that some of the references in the latter part of the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition with regard to the specific instance which was the subject of his previous motion might be deemed so to reflect, but as long as the Leader of

the Opposition confines himself to the competence of officials who are mentioned in these estimates I believe he is in order. Otherwise, if he reflects on a vote, he is, of course, not in order. My difficulty, as hon. members will appreciate, is to draw a very difficult line.
On the point of order, I think the Leader of the Opposition is nearly through.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I would point out that I have already made it clear that the remarks I am making are directed to the offices which are provided for in the estimates themselves. I submit that it is entirely proper and, in fact, the duty of hon. members to discuss subjects of this kind when there can be any possibility that there has been a misinterpretation of what took place in this house and at a time when the subject is bound to come up for further consideration. What I am saying is not and cannot be directed to a motion which has already been dealt with by a vote in one case or to a motion which, in another case, was held not to be immediately debatable. My remarks relate to an office for which provision is made in the estimates, and it is in that light that I am placing these facts before the committee.
I now proceed to deal with the questions arising in connection with the chairman and deputy chairman because the statement to which I refer, which was made by the Minister of Finance, related to the officers of the house whose conduct had been under consideration. I would point out that both the chairman and the deputy chairman repeatedly refused to hear members on points of order or questions of privilege. That is a matter of record in Hansard. It is not going to be erased from Hansard by any suggestion that some motion has been dealt with or another motion not discussed. In fact, so very clear did this become that on one occasion the deputy chairman made it obvious that he was denying the right simply in order to get a vote taken on a motion which was before the committee and before any question as to its impropriety could be raised.
On that occasion, as I think will be recalled by all hon. members who were here at the time, he admitted that the member for Kamloops was correct in stating that the deputy chairman deliberately ignored members who were trying to get the floor and that he ignored them because he intended to put the question without hearing any argument. I refer to Hansard, page 4560, column 2, to indicate the reference I have made. In this course both the chairman and the deputy chairman were in flagrant violation of the

following standing orders or citations: Standing order 17, which provides that whenever any matter of privilege arises it shall be taken into consideration immediately; standing order 34 (1), which provides in effect that a member may raise a point of order at any time; citation 110, Beauchesne, third edition, which points out that points of order are questions raised with the view of calling attention to any departure from the standing orders and the customary modes of proceeding in a debate or in the conduct of legislative business, and may be raised at any time by any member. I would repeat, Mr. Chairman, that the citation is emphatic that these questions may be raised at any time by any member. Nevertheless, members were denied on this occasion.
The deputy chairman permitted consideration of clauses of the bill in committee out of their proper order. He did this by giving a strange interpretation, I might say a fantastic interpretation, to the word "consideration" whereby he found himself able to rule that a clause had been considered by the committee although the minister had done nothing more than give a summary of its content and move its postponement. The whole procedure occupied about 15 seconds. As a result of this misinterpretation there was a breach later of the following standing orders: Standing order 78 (1), which provides that every clause must be considered by the committee in its proper order; standing order 33, the closure rule, which provides that closure will apply only to those matters which have already been considered and that the further consideration of them will not be further postponed. The chairman was able to say, by the unusual procedure he followed, that clauses had been considered which had not actually even been before the committee.
I am not going to make the other references I could make, Mr. Chairman, to the application of other rules, citations and standing orders which are affected by what was done on this occasion. I have simply stated what took place as a question of fact. Hansard will support the statements I have made. I have indicated the applicable standing orders and citations to show where, in our opinion, there was a departure from the procedure which should have been followed. We believe that dangerous precedents have been established as the result of that. We believe that the effectiveness of the positions of the Speaker, the chairman and the deputy chairman have been seriously affected by what has taken place. Therefore at the appropriate time it will be proper to consider what did occur.
What should be remembered, however, at this time, because we now have the whole 67509-335
House of Commons
activity of the government before us on a motion to provide interim supply, is that it was the government which succeeded in having these unfortunate incidents carried to their very definite conclusion. The minister has denied certain statements that appeared in the press about his intervention. The minister has not denied that there was a discussion of what took place in this house with the Speaker. The minister cannot deny that members of the government did discuss with the Speaker what would take place in the house. The minister cannot deny that what happened had the result of changing the whole course of the debate in the house. The minister cannot deny that these were not merely questions of mistakes or otherwise. The minister cannot deny that the effect of what took place was to make it possible for the government to meet a deadline which it had set.
I am raising these points now so that there may be no uncertainty that in dealing with the estimates of the government generally and in dealing with the estimates involving the offices of Speaker, chairman and deputy chairman of committees, we have not for one moment withdrawn in any way from the position we took. We made it perfectly clear when we presented first a motion relating to the chairman and then a motion relating to the Speaker that it was the action of the government which we believed had made these men victims of their course of conduct. We believe that as the result of what happened the government should in honour dissolve at the earliest possible date and make it possible for the house to meet again with a new parliament, whatever the government may be, that will be in harmony and in keeping with the wishes of the people themselves.
If this government were re-elected it would at least come forward then with a mandate to take a new course and to take a fresh stand. If the people of the country elected a new government in such a test, and most certainly that is a possibility which the government has every right to recognize, then this whole situation would be changed by the application of the rules in keeping with our ancient traditions.
We believe that when we spoke in this house during the debate we were speaking for the majority of the people of Canada, no matter what number of members there may be opposite us in the house at this time. We believe that we were speaking in a manner that was consistent with the rights of parliament and with the traditions of our free parliamentary system. We believe that it would be proper, honourable and just that, before he leaves for the conference in

House of Commons
London, the Prime Minister state that it is his intention to dissolve the house at an appropriate date so that there may be an early election in order to give the people of Canada a right to express their opinion not merely upon the strange procedure by which the government advanced money to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited but-what is more important-in order that the people of Canada may be in a position to express their opinion upon the manner in which this government violated the rules and brought the position of Speaker, Deputy Speaker and chairman of committees and deputy chairman of committees into disrepute by the action they were forced to follow as a result of the conduct of the government. That is what I believe would be in keeping with the great traditions of parliament which have been challenged in this way.
When the Minister of Finance talks about the attack made on the Speaker and the chairman of committees, he should remember that he was the one who introduced the motion for the ejection of the hon. member for Eglinton which precipitated one of the scenes in this house which brought to the attention of the Canadian public what had taken place. Oh, when the hon. members opposite make their contemptible insinuations that this was a planned course of action-
It was.

We hear from the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, still sitting in his seat. We hear from him that it was. Does the minister suggest that we knew that the Minister of Finance was going to introduce this motion? What utter nonsense! He was not taking us into his confidence. We did not know that he was going to make himself a party to action of this kind. What happened was the result of the action of the Minister of Finance himself; and when he makes statements such as those he made in his radio address, it would be well if he remembered that.
The question of interim supply, Mr. Chairman, raises the right to discuss many things. We wish that it were possible on this occasion, by dealing with specific items, to raise an issue that could precipitate the kind of vote that would express the opinion of this house with regard to certain detailed matters. But that is not possible. We cannot deal with individual items on this motion for interim supply. As I have said, the motion for interim supply is one which, by tradition, is accepted in this house; and it is accepted in Westminster in the same way. I recognize that there is control over supply by the house. I recognize that in the house the

majority will, of course, decide. But I also recognize that it has been customary, over the years, to grant supply for the purpose of the business of the country. I should like to read a quotation which is perhaps not without some application to this matter. It is to be found in a book entitled "Parliamentary Grants" by Durell. At page 4 he says this:
The drastic step of refusing supplies is, however, one which has never been applied. A sword of Damocles, of which the blade is eaten away with rust, it remains suspended in the armoury of the constitution-an object of historical and picturesque interest alone.
Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, while it may be an object of historical and picturesque interest alone, it provides the opportunity to discuss certain subjects which need to be raised. I have made these remarks at this time because I wish to state once again that what occurred in this house has not been changed by any vote that has been taken. What has occurred in this house has damaged the effectiveness of this parliament as long as the present parliament remains. What has happened in this house under the guidance of this government has damaged the rules and placed on record precedents which at some future time could be extremely dangerous indeed. This government may preen itself that its conduct will be safe for the people of Canada. We do not believe that it is correct in making that assumption. But even if that is the opinion of this government, there could be men of such strange and radical views that they would recognize the danger there could be if these men could toss out the rule books and, by a simple majority, force through this house anything they wanted done.
That was what this government did with the unfortunate co-operation of the Speaker, the chairman of committees and the deputy chairman. That is the reason that these facts need to be repeated. That is the reason that this government no longer has any moral right to govern. That is the reason the Prime Minister would be following the honourable course if he assured us that there would be an election which would cleanse this parliament and bring back a parliament in keeping with the wishes of the people of Canada in relation to this great issue which has developed. It is not a matter of the right of members of parliament as individuals; it is a matter of the rights of the people of Canada. We are only their servants; we are only their representatives. Our right to speak is the right of the people of Canada to be heard. That right has been challenged; and imbedded now in our rules-until there is another parliament-are dangerous precedents which

could be gravely abused at any time by this or any succeeding government.
Before I sit down I want to speak on one other subject which I believe is of immediate importance as a result of what has taken place. On various occasions in the past we have presented resolutions calling for the setting up of an appropriate committee or commission to consider reform of the Senate. Mr. Chairman, I believe that this is a proper time for the Prime Minister to consider the way in which reform of the Canadian Senate can be effectively brought about. Over many long years members of the party which supports him have expressed their belief that there should be reform. We have expressed our belief that there should be reform. There should therefore be agreement on this subject. We agree that, as long as this government remains in office, it must assume the initiative in dealing with this subject. We believe it is one with regard to which the provincial governments must be consulted. It may well be that a royal commission, which embraces representatives of this government and of the provincial governments as well as members of the two houses, should consider this whole subject. Most certainly if ever there was evidence that the other house needs reform, it is now as a result of the way in which the extremely important bill, which was so extensively discussed publicly and in this house, was dealt with in the Senate. That the measure was put through by a new form of overall closure which provided its acceptance in such a speedy and expeditious manner, in keeping with the desires of the government of this country, emphasizes the need for sweeping reforms which will give to the other house an effective part in our bicameral system. The Prime Minister has it in his power to initiate proceedings which could continue, no matter what happens to this government or to any other government. With the evidence before us of what has occurred, I submit that it would be appropriate that these steps be taken now. I raise this question because, if these steps are to be taken, the Prime Minister could be considering them before his departure from, or most certainly before his return to, this house.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I shall give way to other speakers who may wish to discuss other subjects under interim supply. I repeat that in supporting this motion for interim supply we are simply following precedents and that this does not in any way limit our right to question any item; that it in no way prejudices our right to challenge any department; that it in no way prejudices our right to question the conduct of any minister or official under this government. We accept, on the one hand, the conditions stated by the 67509-335*
House of Commons
minister in presenting this motion for a supply of one-twelfth of the total amount which has been asked for in the estimates and we shall permit it to pass after such discussion as may take place on any of the items that are before us.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution before us at the present time is what might be called a routine motion. I would say that there is coming to the government a certain measure of credit in connection with the introduction of this motion, but there is also a considerable measure of discredit in what it is doing at the present time. On the credit side I would point out that the delay in which the government indulged with respect to the last interim supply motion is not being repeated on this occasion. Hon. members are aware that it was not until June 11 that the government brought in a motion for interim supply to provide for money for the month of June. In other words, civil service salaries and wages and payments to members of the armed forces for June 15 were under a certain question mark as late as June 11. On this occasion, however, we are dealing with the question of supply for the month of July. So far as individuals are concerned the first salary cheques that are involved are the cheques of July 15. This being June 22, it is obvious that no question mark arises so far as those salary and wage payments are concerned.
As hon. members will recall, when we were debating interim supply on June 11 I gave a long list of dates showing that across the years it had been the practice to request interim supply some time in the month previous to the month for which interim supply was needed. I am glad to see the government getting back on the rails so far as that aspect of the matter is concerned, in that it is now only June 22 when supply is being sought for the month of July.
However, Mr. Chairman, the very fact that this routine motion, this routine request, is being made in such a routine way, as if everything were quite normal, as if nothing; were wrong, is what in my view is to the discredit of the government. What the government is asking for is not just the money that it needs to pay bills and salaries in the month of July, what the government is asking parliament is for permission to carry on in the routine way just as if there were no question as to its moral authority to continue to govern. In our view, as I stated on behalf of this group on June 11, it is not possible for a free parliament to have done to it some of the things that were done in recent weeks and to carry on in the normal way. It still seems to us that the one honourable way to

House of Commons
deal with the situation that has developed in this parliament is for this parliament to be dissolved and an election to be held.
It is not my purpose to rehash the incidents that took place during May and the early part of June. I am sure it will not be necessary for the hon. member for Rosthern or the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to raise any points of order on what I have to say because I shall talk, not about the past but about the present. It is recognized by yourself, Mr. Chairman, and by all the members of the committee that included in the items one-twelfth of which we are now being asked to vote, are items for the work of parliament. In other words, I have in mind not just the items to which the Leader of the Opposition referred but all the items under legislation which provide for parliament to continue in session. It is my view that the atmosphere in this parliament at this time-true, it is because of things that happened in the past but I am talking about the present-makes it the kind of parliament, the kind of House of Commons in particular, which should be dissolved and replaced by another one.
I feel that we owe this as a duty to the Canadian people. After all we are here not for our own sakes; we are here to be the parliament of the people of Canada. There are certain duties which devolve upon us, and I think one of the duties is to have the kind of atmosphere, the kind of relationships back and forth across this house, in which the business of the country can be properly conducted and our work properly done. I think I can say, without at the moment assessing the blame or indulging in any recriminations, that anyone who .looks objectively at the atmosphere in this House of Commons at this time recognizes that it is not the kind of House of Commons to which the Canadian people are entitled. I put it to the Prime Minister and to the government in those terms. I am not going to do as I have done on occasion and bring forth authorities, citations and rules. I put it to the government in plain, human terms. We all know that the atmosphere that now obtains in this House of Commons is not a satisfactory basis for dealing with the work of the country to which it is our duty to attend.
It does seem to me that even the fact that speeches such as the one just made by the Leader of the Opposition can be made, not to mention the points of order that have been raised on the other side, all underline the fact that the moral authority of this parliament has been taken away from it. It is my view it is the government that robbed this parliament of its moral authority.
[Mr. Knowles.l
Apart from that, the fact of the matter is that moral authority no longer obtains in this house. It is quite clear that the best thing the government can do for the good of parliament and out of loyalty to the interests of the Canadian people is to make arrangements just as soon as possible for this parliament to end and for an election to be held. For that reason, Mr. Chairman, I say that the routine way in which this routine motion is being introduced, without any comment being made by the government as to what its plans are for this session or for the holding of an election, is to its discredit.
I appreciate the fact that no minister rose at the end of the speech of the Leader of the Opposition. In other words, others of us were also given an opportunity to speak. But I hope that the government will not sit this debate out. I hope that someone speaking on behalf of the government will deal with the issues that have been raised, will deal particularly with the question as to the moral authority of this parliament to continue. I say again it is an issue that is greater than the government, greater than any party or greater than the interest of individuals here. It is an issue that is of concern to the Canadian people who have the right to have sitting a parliament with a moral authority such as this parliament does not now possess.
I said, Mr. Chairman, that I would not rehash the things that happened during the pipe line debate but that I would deal with the present situation. I hope I will not be accused of breaking that promise because of what I am going to say now. I want to make one reference to something the Minister of Finance said in his radio speech last Friday night and I make it because it seems to me it underlines my contention that the present situation is an unhappy one. I shall not go into the details of the speech he made. I am glad we live in the kind of country where he had the freedom last Friday night, as I had the same freedom a couple of weeks earlier, to express to the people of Canada by radio our views on what is happening here in parliament; but it did seem to me the minister made a very revealing statement when he told the Canadian people over a trans-Canada network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that the purpose of the closure rule is to make it possible to bring to an end a protracted debate-and I emphasize this latter point-or to enable the government to meet a timetable.
That is the revised version.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am talking about the present and I will not talk about the past or how the closure rule was used in the pipe-line debate. We have had a new rule given to us by the Minister of Finance who is the house leader. He has announced it to the entire country. We have had it announced that on any occasion when the government feels it must meet a timetable, or when it wants to meet a timetable, or when it has committed itself to some private corporation that it will meet a timetable, it has the right to resort to the use of the closure rule.
One of the strange things about rules-and I have discovered this in discussing rules with people outside of parliament who are showing more interest in them than they used to-is that all the rules of parliament are not contained in the standing orders. The rules of parliament consist in the standing orders and in the way in which those standing orders have been interpreted. That is the reason we get into these long debates. That is also the reason such big books as Beauchesne's third edition-and many others including May, Bourinot, Campion and all the rest- get printed. The fact is that the practices of parliament are determined not only by the simple clear-cut rules in our standing orders but by precedent and by interpretation. We now have a new interpretation and so far as the government is concerned it is just as much a part of our way of doing things here as if it were spelled out in the standing orders themselves.
I remind the Minister of Finance that actually there is nothing in standing order No. 33, the closure rule, which says what its purpose is. I accept the first part of his statement that the purpose of the closure rule is to enable the government to bring to an end a protracted debate. The reason I accept it is because, like the Minister of Finance, I have read just about everything there is to read concerning the closure rule. I have read in full the debate that took place in 1913 when the rule was written into our standing orders. I have read practically all the debates in which closure was applied in 1913, 1917, 1921, 1926 and 1932.
Mr. Chairman, nowhere in any of the vast amount of material that can be read on closure did any one ever suggest that the purpose of the closure rule was to enable the government to meet a timetable. Plenty of authorities, including Sir Robert Borden who introduced the closure rule, Mr. Arthur Meighen who appears to have had something to do with drafting it, and others who have used it across the years, admit, claim and affirm that its purpose is to enable the government to bring to an end a protracted debate.
House of Commons
When those who gave birth to the rule and used it in previous sessions referred to it they gave as examples of protracted debate, two, three or five weeks on one clause of a bill. The occasions when it was used in the past, except for the most recent past, were occasions when debate had gone on for weeks or even months. In other words, Mr. Chairman, until 1956 there was no question about it; the only purpose of the closure rule was to enable the government to bring to an end a protracted debate and there was no question but that "protracted" meant weeks or months.
Now, however, we have the precedent established in the recent debate when the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave notice of closure at the end of the first speech at the first stage of the debate, plus all the precedents in the recent debate regarding closure, and in addition to that we have this interpretation given by the Minister of Finance: Any time the government is in a jam as to a timetable, any time the government has to meet a commitment it has made to someone else, it is justified in using the closure rule, because the Minister of Finance, the house leader, has personally told the country that is its purpose.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I say this parliament cannot continue under the direction of a government which thinks in those terms. I had dared to hope-yes, even I had dared to hope-that the government had learned some lessons because of the experiences we went through in the month of May and the early part of June of this year. If the government was not impressed by the arguments we were making from this side of the house I had hoped that it would have been impressed by the editorial comments in newspapers across the country, particularly editorial comments in newspapers like the Toronto Star and the Winnipeg Free Press which have been well known as supporters of the Liberal party across the years.
Lo and behold, Mr. Chairman, despite all these editorials, despite all the reasons we might have had to believe the government would have learned its lesson and realized that it cannot wound parliament and go on as if nothing had happened, when it is all over the Minister of Finance takes to the radio and announces to the people of Canada a new rule: From here on any time one man in the cabinet wants something that means meeting a timetable which is inconvenient for parliament, we have the right to use the closure rule.
Well, Mr. Chairman, it is perfectly true there is nothing in the rule that says the government cannot use it for that purpose. The rule does not state what its purpose is

House of Commons
either one way or the other but parliament is governed, as Beauchesne points out on one of his earlier pages, not only by its standing orders but by its traditions, practices and precedents, and by the interpretations placed on its rules and standing orders across the years.
Until this recent occasion there was no question as to what the interpretation of the closure rule was but now we have this disgraceful precedent which we went through so far as the use of closure is concerned in May and June of 1956; and we have this equally disgraceful interpretation which my friend the Minister of Finance has placed on the closure rule.
As hon. members are aware there are other aspects of the present situation into which I could go but I shall avoid confusing the issue at this time. It seems to me, in addition to the atmosphere in which we find ourselves, that this one point in the minister's speech which I have emphasized is an indication that the government feels it is authorized to take dictatorial action quite properly. Because that is not so, I think it is clear that this parliament should not continue.
As I indicated on June 11 in so far as interim supply involves the provision of money for the government to pay civil service salaries and wages, we shall of course support the bill, preserving the rights of any other members who wish to speak on this motion today and preserving also our right to discuss all of the items in the estimates as they come before us during whatever period this session continues. Nevertheless it is still our view, as I indicated on the occasion of the last interim supply motion, that the government does not have the moral authority to ask this of parliament in a routine way just as if everything had got back to normal. It has not got back to normal. The only way in which parliament can be restored to the position of moral authority which it requires to carry on its business is for this House of Commons to be dissolved and a new one elected.
Mr. Chairman, we are not in the position today on June 22-it should be borne in mind that we are discussing salaries to be paid on July 15-that we were in on June 11. As some newspapers have pointed out, the opposition had it chosen to do so could have forced the government that date into a very tight corner. Some newspapers even suggested that the opposition could have forced the government into an election.
We are not in that position today. We are not able to use what might be called force. We are putting it to the government on a straight moral basis as an appeal-I have

strong suspicions that there are those on the government side who agree with us-that it would be better for parliament, better for Canada if the scenes we witnessed here and the experiences through which we have gone, and the atmosphere that now obtains, were wiped out by the dissolution of this parliament and the election of a new one with the moral authority to serve the interests of the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, before I proceed to discuss what I had intended to discuss on this occasion it becomes my responsibility and privilege to set forth in a few words the general attitude of the Social Crediters in this house respecting the subjects and the situations with which the Leader of the Opposition has dealt today at considerable length, and in connection with which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has made certain additional remarks.
We Social Crediters feel that the government has brought this interim supply resolution before the committee in good time. We think there is nothing wrong or unusual or immoral in asking for interim supply in this manner and at this time. Hence this committee should pass the resolution after reasonable discussion.
There is a matter which I should like to raise which affects my constituency and I presume a good many others in the country. I should like to read a telegram which came to my office. It is dated June 15, 1956 and reads:
John Blackmore,
Member of Parliament.
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
Lethbridge confronted with serious shortage of mortgage money for housing can possibly mean 50 per cent labour layoff within 60 days your assistance urgently required.
Arthur L. Batty,
First Vice-President,
Lethbridge House Builders Association.
I suppose a telegram similar to that has reached nearly every hon. member of this house. I feel most unhappy about the condition which has developed in Lethbridge. I have already raised the question of the effect upon my constituency brought about by the increase in the rediscount rate by the Bank of Canada. I believe that the particular conditions which have been brought about in my constituency are absolutely and unqualifiedly unjustified in this country. If with all our modem means of managing finance we cannot prevent a suspected inflation in the country as a whole, without practically crucifying various parts of that country, then

it is high time we adopted a different course in the management of the banks of this country.
Only this morning I received a letter which contains a statement indicating the kind of thing which has been brought about in certain other areas. This letter comes from Willowdale, Ontario, but it refers to conditions which exist in a constituency represented by an hon. member. The letter reads:
Do you appreciate what the sudden curtailing of credit by banks and other financial institutions has done to the small builders of homes and their sub-contractors? The following is a typical example. John Doe of North York used to build four houses at a time. Previous to June 15th he had never experienced difficulty in obtaining mortgages. When he couldn't arrange mortgages on the last four he started building he couldn't pay his subcontractors who had made the excavation, put in the footings, put on the floor joists and rough floor and done his brickwork and put on the roof. Because he couldn't pay the sub-contractors they couldn't pay their men, nor could they meet their payments on cars, trucks and equipment. One sub-contractor was only a few days overdue on his payment on his truck. He was working on my house when the finance company's bailiff seized it. I saved him by loaning him $50. If I hadn't he would have lost his truck, equipment and his means of earning a living.
May I interpolate, because of action on the part of the Bank of Canada! No effort has been made to prevent people being distressed by the seizure of their property. The letter continues:
Economic conditions in North York are getting chaotic. Thus we see the international bankers ordering the national banks to call loans and restrict credits on the pretence that it is to halt inflation. All it does is shake down the little man. He is forced to liquidate many of his assets at half their value-
May I interpolate again, so that people who are interested in high finance in this country can buy them at half price, thereby enriching themselves to the extent to which the poor man is impoverished. The letter continues:
-or lose everything he has because the banks suddenly and without warning shut off his normal credit. In other words the international bankers have ordered the Bank of Canada to create conditions which play right into the hands of the communist leaders in this and other so-called free countries. All the working men and little contractors are blaming the government for their present misfortune. May I ask what their elected representatives intend to do about it. So far I haven't been able to arrange a mortgage on my home although several real estate agents have appraised it as being worth $15,800. One big mortgage company told me "we are now restricted to giving mortgages on houses valued at over $25,000".
Before I unfortunately had to go away for two weeks, I heard one or two members of the banking and commerce committee, of which I am a member, who represented such
Interim Supply
areas complain about this very situation. But no ear was turned, no consideration was given to their complaints; these things were just shaken off as being just "one of those things". As far as I am concerned, the misfortunes which are being inflicted upon the Lethbridge constituency are not "just one of those things". Those are misfortunes which are deliberately brought on by the Bank of Canada at the instigation of international banking concerns. Until it can be proved otherwise, I make that statement, positive that I can prove it if given time.
We have heard already a statement, which I am not able to document to the date, but we have heard a statement that there is a trend in Canada toward greater international control of our finances. That is exactly the abomination which was attempted when we accepted the Bretton Woods agreement. We in Canada were no longer big enough and wise enough to manage our own financial system.
The first bank of this country was managed at a little place in New Brunswick, just a small province, and they got along splendidly. They did not have to have anyone from London or New York interfering with their affairs, to tell them how or how not to manage their bank and their economy. They could get along very well. They helped their people to finance production and consumption. They protected those who depended on their bank. In the light of that, can anyone conceive of a reason why the great Dominion of Canada in the year 1956, with all the economic power that it possesses and with all the experience it has had in banking, cannot run its own affa 'r I financially? Now I think I have said enouj it
Hear, hear.

There are several people who want this closed off. Several people In the banking and commerce committee wanted this discussion closed off, but the simple fact of the matter is that the members of this house have the responsibility to see that this kind of thing is not closed off and that this kind of abomination is rectified before it goes too far. That is exactly the kind of thing that happened in communities all over the country when the great depression came. As a result of the first moves toward the great depression the wheels started running downhill, and no one knew how to stop them from running further downhill. We had the most terrible experience during the depression. We do not want to get into that condition again. We want the wheels to be running on the right hill, and we want the right wheels, and run by the right people.

Interim Supply
I urge the minister to see that something is done without further delay to rectify the financial conditions existing in the Lethbridge constituency. It is not a minor constituency of this country; it is one of the best economic areas in Canada. It has splendid resources, splendid businessmen and splendid businesses, and it has fine industrial equipment up to a point. There is no reason why the city and district of Lethbridge should be plunged into a depression by some action down here in Ottawa. In the depression of 1935, when we came here to Ottawa and began telling the house the troubles we were having, most of the members in this house sitting on the Liberal side shrugged their indifferent shoulders and indicated that it was our own fault and that it was our own business to get ourselves out of the uifficulty. Now we have got ourselves out of the difficulty, they want to push us back in again. This has gone too far, and so I ask the minister once more, not necessarily that he speak here, but that he speak to the right people of Canada to rectify the financial difficulties, not only of the people of Lethbridge constituency, but of the people all over Canada.
Since it is about three minutes to one, may I call it one o'clock?
Go on.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it agreed that I call it one o'clock?
No.

Well, if you want me to put in time for three minutes, I do not intend to begin what I am going to say now and break it off at one o'clock. So if you want me to stand here and put in time for three minutes, I shall stand here. Shall we call it one o'clock?
No.

I thought the speech the Leader of the Opposition gave this morning was one of the most thoughtful, one of the most well-directed, and one of the most concise speeches I have ever heard given in this house. It was a good lesson in directness, pointedness and in background for all Liberal members of the house. For instance, the Leader of the Opposition was able to stand up and say what he feels, directly and clearly, without any fear that he should not say certain things because they might hurt sensitive feelings, whereas when Liberal members speak they have to keep looking over their shoulders to see what the Minister of Trade and Commerce is thinking about them or what the Minister of Finance is saying. Even the Prime Minister used to cast dagger looks at some
[Mr. Blackmore.l
of these figures, but he has pretty well stopped doing that now because he is leaving things to other people to look after. But I thought the speech this morning by the Leader of the Opposition was a marvel of clarity and of directness.
You are best known for your sincerity.
He told the government exactly what he thought in the minimum number of words.
Oh.

There was no doubt in anybody's mind of what he wanted to say, and he certainly said it.
May I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to discuss for a moment the matter brought up this morning by the Leader of the Opposition regarding the phrase which the Minister of Trade and Commerce used on the television program "Press Conference" a week ago last night. There were many of us who listened to that program, and at that time we heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce clearly say: "We violated the rules."
No, no.

I have spoken to the gentlemen who interviewed the Minister of Trade and Commerce on that program and they are unanimously of the opinion that he used those words. All of them were very surprised that he should have used such a phrase and they discussed it among themselves afterwards. Mr. Bain said to the minister, "I was very surprised to hear you say 'we violated the rules' ". Mr. Bain says that the minister said, "Oh, did I say that?"
To make absolutely sure, Mr. Chairman, that my ears had not deceived me I have just spent the last hour or so at the C.B.C. studio and I have heard played back several times their recording of what was said during that press conference. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said: "We violated the rules".
"No rules".

A tape recording has been made for me by the C.B.C. and it will be in this building very shortly. In fact, I am advised by my colleague the hon. member for York West that the recording is here now and I cordially invite any minister or any hon.

member who would like to hear the voice of the Minister of Trade and Commerce clearly say, "we violated the rules", to listen to him say it in the opposition lobby right now. That will clear up this whole matter for all time. It will clear up the Prime Minister's attempt to mislead the house with regard to this matter and also the very direct attempt this morning of the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he denied having said these very damaging words. As I say, if there is any doubt in anybody's mind the tape recording made by the C.B.C. in the last hour from their own recording of the proceedings that took place on that evening is in the opposition lobby for anyone who wishes to listen to it. So let us have no more-
Oh, go out and entertain yourself.
I have entertained myself very much listening to the Minister of Trade and Commerce say what I said he said.

I heard it and he did not
say it.
Then I invite you to go out into the opposition lobby and hear him say it over again for your benefit. Go ahead. You see, that is what we run up against. Ministers make statements-
May I ask a question?
Certainly.
Would the hon. gentleman excuse me? I would prefer to go out and hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce rather than to listen to the hon. member.
That suits me very well because I do not think-
You do not think, period.
-that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has ever added to the proceedings of this house either while speaking or while listening.
More than you.
A great deal.

I see that the member for St. Lawrence-St. George cannot even make up his own mind on the little matter of whether or not he will leave the house. He said definitely he would. Then he went outside and said to himself, "My gosh, maybe I have not done the right thing. I might miss something." So he turned right around and came back in. Now he is going out again. He cannot decide whether he wants to stay in or go out.

He will not miss much.
House of Commons

That is a good example of the kind of decisions that are made on the other side of the house. The statement that the Minister of Trade and Commerce made, "we violated the rules", is nothing new in this house as far as the government is concerned, this tired, old gang of power-hungry politicians, because that is the concept of government that the cabinet has been developing over the past few years. That concept simply is that if the rules suit the government the government will abide by the rules, but if the rules do not suit the government they will change the rules without allowing one word of protest, one question of privilege, one point of order to be raised. They will summon their majority and by using the rule of might makes right they will bring about whatever rule change suits their desire at the moment.
During the pipe line debate we saw rules of parliamentary procedure that have been built up over several hundred years in the British parliament and during the past hundred years in this parliament thrown out the window. They did not suit the government's purpose. It became very clear that if a rule impeded the will of the government the government would simply change the rule. That is how dictatorships are born. That is how dictatorship became a reality in this chamber in the last few weeks. Of course, this could only be made possible by the complete subordination of the chair by the cabinet, and that all who were in the chamber during that debate or who were sitting in the galleries very clearly saw.
Oh, speak for yourself.
I am speaking for myself. I am at least doing what no Liberal member is allowed to do in this house. I am speaking my own views without fear of-
Of what?
-being told that I do not have the right to stand up and speak my views. I am doing exactly what the hon. member for Timiskaming has advised me to do.
What happened when the hon. member for Calgary South tried to get up to speak on the Tory roster?
When the hon. member for Calgary South rose to speak he was allowed to speak, and-
He was cut off.
-he was listened to. I believe he spoke oftener than any other Conservative member.

Oh, oh!

House of Commons

The Tories tried to cut
him off.

I should like to ask the voluble Minister of Fisheries why more people on his side of the house, more Liberal members, did not have the courage to get up on their feet and speak on behalf of this measure that the government jammed down the throats of members of parliament and the Canadian people.
Fifty-three members did.

I noticed that the minister confined all his remarks to heckling and speaking from his seat. He did not have the courage to stand up and speak on behalf of the measure he heralded so widely. He simply sat and, with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, confined his contribution to snide remarks made from the security of a large majority and while sitting in his seat.
Fifty-three Liberals spoke; eight ministers.

As I have said, Mr. Chairman, the creation of this dictatorship in parliament was only made possible by the complete subordination of the Chair to the wishes of the government. It is very obvious that between ten o'clock on the night of Thursday, May 31, and eleven o'clock on the morning of Friday, June 1, a gun was put to the head of the Speaker and probably the Deputy Speaker. There is no doubt that the Speaker was told either to toe the line along with the rest of his colleagues or that his future in the Liberal party was through. It was a very difficult decision for any man to make, but by means of that threat he was obviously forced by the government to do their bidding. When he stood up at eleven o'clock on Friday morning, June 1, black Friday as far as this parliament is concerned, he carried out completely the orders of the government.
During the whole debate the operation of ;he telegraph system between the Minister of Finance, under the dictation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and whoever happened to be the occupant of the chair at any particular time, was very obvious. During the expulsion of the hon. member for Eglinton it was obvious that all moves were dictated by the Minister of Finance. During most of the rest of the debate the Chair obeyed the dictates of the government and the messages were conveyed to the Chair through the Minister of Finance.
What the people of Canada thought of the government's conduct in bringing in and jamming this pipe-line bill down the throats of parliament and of the Canadian people, their conduct in parliament, and the conduct they forced upon parliament was very clearly

revealed by two Gallup polls, one taken immediately before the debate and one taken immediately after it.
I think these results are interesting. Immediately before the debate the Gallup poll reported the following: Of all the people asked which party they would support if a general election were held on that day, 48 per cent of the people said they would vote Liberal, 30 per cent Conservative, 13 per cent C.C.F. and 7 per cent Social Credit. In the poll immediately after this debate took place, these were the results: 43 per cent said they would vote Liberal, 34 per cent said they would vote Conservative, 15 per cent said they would vote C.C.F. and 6 per cent said they would vote Social Credit. Hence as a result of this debate the Liberal party lost 5 points, dropping from 48 to 43. The Conservatives picked up 4 points, going from 30 to 34. The C.C.F. who opposed the government alongside the Conservative party picked up 2 points, going from 13 to 15. The Social Credit party-quite deservedly for having tagged along hanging on to the coattails of the Liberal party on this matter-lost 1 of their few points; they dropped from 7 to 6. So, Mr. Chairman, that shows you what the people of Canada thought of the pipe line bill and of the way in which the government conducted itself in jamming it down the throats of parliament and the people of Canada.
Tell us about Saskatchewan.

Do I hear some bold Liberals talking about any of the three provincial elections that just took place? Surely not. I am sure my ears deceived me. I am sure they would not speak of those sad matters at this present time. So, Mr. Chairman, I back up completely what my leader said this morning in dealing with this matter. I think that the opinions expressed by the people of Canada, as shown by the latest Gallup poll, describe more clearly than can any words just what the people of Canada think of the measure which this government has recently jammed through parliament and of the conduct of that party and this government in bending the rules to suit their wishes of the moment.

Our guest is the Rt. Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Trade and Commerce. Our chairman is Robert McKeown, Ottawa editor of Weekend magazine. Members of the press are George Bain of the Toronto Globe and Mail, Arthur McKenna, Ottawa correspondent of the Wall Street Journal and Canadian Dow-Jones, and Stanley Burke of the Vancouver Sun.

Do you take the position that all the procedural wrangle that there was in the House of Commons was mere obstruction and wasn't based on violation of rules or attempted violation of rules by the government?
Howe: Oh no, we violated the rules.

Oh, the record out there reveals the truth. Just go out and listen to it.

We-the closure is, well, it is in the rule book, it is put there-even Angus Maclnnis said that it is the duty of the government to use it in the face of obstruction.
Those are all the words, but the material words are that admission and confession by the minister,-and he could do no other, Mr. Chairman-"We violated the rules". When the minister today denied having made that statement, it was either on the basis 67509-336i
