of the fact that he was trying to delude the house or he may have conveniently forgotten words that were heard everywhere in Canada, words that gave supporting evidence-if that was needed at all-of the fact that they had indeed violated the rules as they have never before been violated at any time in the history of representative government. I also note that he made a reference to myself -and I shall refer to that-at page 14 where he used these words:
We anticipated the delaying tactics-the obstruction-and you remember that before the bill was ever debated, Mr. Coldwell stated that his party would obstruct by every known way in the rule book, and Mr. Diefenbaker stated that this would be the filibuster of filibusters, and you remember it took us several hours to even get the bill- to get the resolution introduced.
Mr. Chairman, I do not often deny statements that are made, whether loose or untrue.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is not safe.

But the statement in question by my right hon. friend is not based on the facts. I have before me the only reference that I ever made outside of this house to the question and I read it now because I read it then during the course of a radio broadcast. The broadcast was given in the month of March. This is what I said:
In July, 1955, the Conservative party fought, under the inspiring leadership and generalship of George Drew, for the restoration of parliamentary supremacy. That was when Mr. Howe tried to force through parliament the grant to himself of a blank cheque of absolute and dictatorial powers, under the Defence Production Act.
That battle we won.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: This one you lost.
I beg the minister's pardon?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The next one you lost.

My right hon. friend says we lost the last one. We did so. They changed the rules between innings. They threw the rule book out. They did not dare to trust to the ordinary, traditional procedure of parliament. We lost the last one in parliament. We will give you an opportunity -as you were challenged to do over and over again-to go to the country now and let the people decide with regard to this matter.
What about Saskatchewan?

You answered us in
parliament with your majority of automatons that jumped at your command. But no government in all the history of this country has ever been so taunted and challenged to go to the country as has this

House of Commons
government in the last two weeks. How do they meet it? They meet it with fear, maintaining silence.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: How could anyone look across this aisle and fear?

I will deal with that in a few minutes when I finish this quotation. I said:
That battle we won.
That was one time when the Prime Minister was able to do what, in his heart of hearts, he has wanted to do and that is uphold parliament. It could only be done after my hon. friend went on a fishing trip. Then, when the hon. gentleman was away, parliament won. This pipe line debate took place at a time when the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not think it convenient to go on such a trip. I continue the quotation:
But let me tell you that the fight we put on then will appear but a skirmish beside the battle we shall wage when the bill regarding Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, comes before parliament.
Those are the remarks I made. Nowhere was there any mention of a filibuster.
Now, you are getting funny.

There was a declaration that the opposition was going to take its stand on behalf of the rights of parliament and on behalf of the things in which it believes. None of us expected then that this government would ever have done what it did. It tore up the rule book. Three hundred years ago a representative of the crown removed from the Journals record two pages concerning two certain dates. In this case all the government did, with the assistance of the Speaker, was simply something that can only take place in one part of the world and that is when crossing the international date line in an easterly direction; they said today is yesterday.
Yes, we have challenged you to go to the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: In a feeble kind of a way.

Feeble? What must we do? Tear up the rules and walk over there and shove you out? Is that what you want? We simply say to you, you dare not do it. You are afraid. You are silent. You tore up the rules and you destroyed the constitution. You did all those things. But, sir, never before has a government with such an overwhelming majority, as numerous as the sands of the sea, been taunted, challenged and dared so frequently. But there they sit.

The interruptions in which they indulge are all we get. They dare not take the chance.
Now, sir, I am going to make a suggestion. We realize that the Minister of Finance is a great believer in cyclical budgeting, at least he inherited the mantle of the former minister and was a member of the government that brought forth the proposition that cyclical budgeting was indeed the essence of good parliamentary procedure. Cyclical budgeting in the last seven or eight years has consisted of reducing taxes just before an election. You reduced taxation in 1949 just before the election. I think some income taxes went down 30 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And in 1955.

In 1953; we will deal with that in a moment. In 1949 there was a big cut. Then, came the election with the attendant success and up went taxes. There was nothing more heard about it until 1953 when, as if again by coincidence, taxation was reduced. The trivial reductions in 1955 are meaningless. They do not win elections. This is my suggestion. If all you want is the opportunity to reduce taxation, to hold out the bait that you held out in 1949 and in 1953, let us have a baby budget. You will have the opportunity now to introduce one and also to interlard it with promises of health insurance. Bring those things in right now, and then go to the country. You will have all the benefits, all the advantages of cyclical budgeting. Besides that you will be able to go to the country now at a time when things are so favourable to you as you contend. We will support your baby budget. We will help it through. Then, you will have no other excuse for not going to the country.
They dare not go, Mr. Chairman; they know that across Canada the people are aroused as never before.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The voice of Saskatchewan.

My hon. friend should not speak about that. The voice of Saskatchewan did not say anything particularly favourable to the Liberal party. The only thing it showed was that the ambitious plans and the promises of a few weeks ago were dissipated in the light of experience.
I again suggest this. Do not worry about Saskatchewan. You might also think of the province of New Brunswick. Some of my hon. friends over there are the ones who made such a magnificent contribution in the province of Quebec a few days ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: It was much better than the Tories in Saskatchewan.
Not very much better.
How about the Tories in New Brunswick?

My hon. friend the minister interrupted me a moment ago. I say this for him. He was the last to see the light in the province of Quebec. He finally went down against his better judgment, and he and the other ministers who went into Quebec found that their interference there brought them dividends which they certainly did not expect. They were just going to wipe out that government.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: You do not know how to read the newspapers. You do not know what happened in my own constituency.
You get up and tell us what happened.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I will.
I think my hon. friend the minister often trades in his constituency and that was the result that was achieved in his own constituency. But go to the country now.
Who was elected in Prince Albert?

I have often thought of my hon. friend the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration as a "Gliberal". He would believe anything twice, as Mencken once said. My suggestion is this. This parliament has lost its prestige. This parliament no longer speaks in accents of authority. This parliament no longer represents the integrity and dignity of the people of Canada. These things cannot be achieved by this institution in its piesent form, and I say that in no partisan sense.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends laugh. This is but a hollow shell of its former self. It has been discredited as no other parliament has been by the malicious actions of this government, two or three ministers, all of whom have contributed to reducing it to possible servitude because of the majority the government possesses. The Minister of Trade and Commerce with unaccustomed truthfulness admitted to the people the other day: "We violated-
No rules.
-the rules. Mr. Chairman, the Scriptures speak of those who have ears and cannot hear. Let those of you who have ears of that kind go out into the lobby and listen and be convinced.

You got that out of the almanac.
House of Commons
Ask the C.B.C., which made the recording.
I have the C.B.C. recording here. Out in the lobby is the recording-
Made by the C.B.C.
-made by the C.B.C., the sacred instrument which is under the direction of the Minister of National Revenue, and I say that with great respect for the C.B.C.
It is the first time you have ever had any respect for it.

Is that so? The C.B.C. does not deceive. I ask the Minister of National Revenue to go out in the lobby and get a photostatic copy by ear. He knows something about photostats and in the lobby he can get a photostatic copy by ear of what the Minister of Trade and Commerce actually said.
Go out and get educated.

When I mention photostats, Mr. Chairman, I speak of a subject I know the Minister of National Revenue will remember as long as he has memory.
Bring in the baby budget; bring in the taxes; make an alteration of the tax now imposed in connection with the C.B.C. Go to the country; see if we cannot restore this institution and give it a heart and soul, such as it used to have, rather than leaving it as it is, an empty shell consisting only of individuals; a parliament deprived of its great dignity, emasculated as a result of the actions of men who although they hold ministerial positions and give lip service to democracy have attempted to destroy it in the last few weeks.
I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance what would happen to justice in this country if every time you had a court case that was difficult you were permitted to say, "The rules of evidence do not apply here; let us set them aside. After all, we cannot win under the rules and that being so let us alter the rules or destroy them if necessary." I ask the minister how long justice would prevail in our country under those circumstances? How long would order exist? How long would decency be preserved? That is exactly what has happened here in this house. No one who went through the experience of two or three weeks ago can ever again feel as those of us who respect parliament felt concerning this institution, which was great in its achievements in the past regardless of what party was in power.
The Leader of the Opposition said that the Minister of Finance dared not deny collaboration on his part with the Speaker. He would

House of Commons
not deny that ministers saw the Speaker between Thursday evening and Friday morning when the Speaker came into the chair. "Government and Parliament" by Herbert Morrison, regarding the Speaker in England, says:
. . . but upon being appointed Speaker he rigorously cuts off his party affiliations. He declares his honourable intention of being the impartial servant of the house as a whole and that in particular he will do his best to safeguard the rights of minorities.
Today the Minister of Finance was given the opportunity by the Leader of the Opposition to deny that he had contributed his helpful co-operation to the Speaker-or that some ministers did-between 10 o'olock on Thursday evening and 11 o'clock on Friday morning. When the minister did not deny that today the whole picture became perfectly clear, a picture that is a negation of what parliamentary government should be. When a man in the high and honourable position of Speaker finds himself subject to the suggestions and the direct or indirect influence of ministers of the crown, such a thing reveals in its naked awfulness what happened to parliament only three weeks ago.
We vote you interim supply on this occasion-
.

Mr. Chairman, we have heard a great deal this afternoon as to whether or not the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that we-meaning the government-violated the rules of this house. As I listened today I wondered if perhaps it is not rather irrelevant whether or not the minister said that because I am sure no one, and least of all the Minister of Trade

and Commerce, would presume to think of him as an authority on parliamentary procedure. I would think it would be very doubtful whether or not the minister would know if the rules had been violated. However, from the investigations I have made among those people who were present at the broadcast, I have no doubt whatever in my mind that the minister did say it, but I think there is a reasonable possibility that it was a slip of the tongue. But I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if it was the sort of slip of the tongue that psychologists would call a Freudian slip, and if the minister's subconscious forced him against his will to speak the truth.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think that slip of the tongue on the part of the minister also reveals a very dangerous attitude on the part of too many members of the cabinet opposite. I have an idea that somehow or another they have developed some rather dangerous conceptions of the role of parliament and its place in our national life.
I suppose most of us realize that here in this institution we are obliged to operate to some extent on the basis of a number of fictions, shall I say, although necessary fictions. They are perhaps somewhat the same sort of fictions by which a wise and prudent wife maintains the institution of matrimony, being so very careful not to reveal to the vulgar eye the realities behind that institution because if she did the institution would collapse.
I have listened with great interest over the past few weeks to citations of precedents in our parliament reaching back many centuries into the past. It has occurred to me on a number of occasions that these references were in some measure irrelevant to the present situation because parliament is not a static institution, it is an evolving institution. The time is not so far distant since the whole role of parliament was that of an opposition, opposition to the executive power of the crown which up until the beginning of the 18th century rested entirely outside the legislative body.
However, we find a different situation now, we have the executive power of the crown brought right into the legislature and those who wield it becoming part of that legislature. For that reason we have, as I say, a number of necessary fictions, necessary because there is always a possibility that the occasion may arise when the fiction has to be made into reality. One of those fictions of course is that parliament decides things. We all know that that is not really the actual truth. I think it is safe to say that we have reached the point where not even the majority actually decides.

The time may come at any moment when members of parliament, particularly the members who support the government, may be faced with such a situation that they have to use these powers which are now largely fictional. For that reason we have to be most careful about preserving these fictions in our parliamentary life. We have to be careful not to expose the real nature of parliament for most of its time and for that reason the government of the day has laid on it a particularly onerous responsibility, to walk delicately like Agag and not to create a situation in which the general public is revealed that not only are the opposition members in the House of Commons powerless against the government majority, but they must also not reveal to the public the fact that in order to maintain the stability of the government the members who support that government must do so willy-nilly.
There is a third responsibility on the government, and this is particularly applicable to Canada in distinction from the mother of parliaments, that is that the government must at all times and at all costs make sure that it does not place the presiding officer of this institution in such a position that he may be charged with partiality in his decisions. Those I think are the responsibilities that a government has and I have the feeling that our present government has fallen into the very bad habit of imagining that the sole role of parliament is to implement and endorse the policies and decisions of the executive. I think that is a most dangerous position for them to take.
It is understandable why this government has fallen into that position. For one thing, it has been in office for a great many years. For another thing, it has a large and overwhelming majority in the house. Another- I am going to mention again the particular factor in this government which I mentioned earlier in the session-is the make-up of the present government. When I say these things I do not want them to be interpreted as criticisms of individual members of the government, but I do want to point out that when many of the leading and most influential members of the government have reached their positions not by the traditional parliamentary route, there is very grave danger to the whole institution of parliament, very grave danger I think to the life and vigour of the party which supports the government.
Not only that, there is great danger-I think this danger has been realized to a great extent today-that we have in the House of Commons, wielding part of the executive power of the crown, ministers who have not
House of Commons
been trained and acclimatized in parliamentary life, who have not had the necessary discipline of sitting as private members for a period of time and in this instance-this is no one's fault but that of the electorate-have not had the necessary discipline of sitting as private members of the opposition. I suggest to you that a government which has not gone through the traditional processes of parliamentary life is greatly endangering the future value and viability of this institution.
I believe seriously that if the present tendency continues much longer no one in this chamber will be in position to rise, as the Leader of the Opposition rose this morning, and suggest that there should be reforms in the other chamber. It is quite on the cards today that members of this house may be reduced to, shall we say, innocuous desuetude, as members in other places are commonly supposed to be. So for that reason I think the government should seriously consider what has happened in this parliament in recent weeks and realize that no matter what the measure was which they wished to pass through this chamber, no matter how valuable they might think it to be for the benefit of the people of Canada, the price they paid for it has been far too high.
Others have spoken today of the atmosphere in this house now. I do not think any objective observer can deny the fact that it is an unhappy atmosphere. There are some bitternesses and some resentments on both sides of the house. There are some doubts as to the moral right of this chamber to continue because of what has happened. I believe that if this government shoulders its major responsibility, and this I consider to be its major responsibility-the major responsibility of any government in a democratic society is the maintenance and support of democratic institutions-then it will leave no stone unturned to undo what has been done.
I suppose it is true to say that no one is particularly impressed with the efficiency of a democratic parliament as a means of carrying out positive policies. Someone has said that it would not exist at all were it not for the fact that other alternatives to it are far less desirable. I think that is true. With all its faults it is the best we can evolve, but to be maintained in public prestige-after all that is a most important factor in parliamentary life, that parliament should enjoy public prestige-it is most important that no steps should be taken in this chamber which cause doubts to rise in the minds of the public as to whether or not they are really represented in this chamber, whether they support the government party or the opposition.

For that reason I seriously urge the government to consider dealing with this situation in the only way it can be dealt with, and that is to give us a new parliament. I do not wish to rehash the past, but I should like to point out that as things stand at present the presiding officer of this chamber is left in an impossible position. Before the much-debated motion was moved the Prime Minister and, I believe, the Minister of Finance expressed the view in this chamber that permitting that motion to go to a vote would not solve any problem. I do not think that situation has changed at all. I think we are still in that situation.
I submit to you, sir, that if this parliament continues for another session it can only do so at the cost of a further decline in the prestige of parliamentary institutions in the eyes of the Canadian public, and I do not think we stand very high today. I would suggest to the government that they should accept as their major responsibility today the reinforcement of this focus of our democratic society, this House of Commons chamber.

I do not propose to continue the analysis of the situation which I feel has been ably summed up by my friend and colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo. Because of the fact that the Minister of Justice has regrettably been absent through illness and because of the fact that the Minister of Labour is absent on a mission, which we hope he will enjoy, in London, I should like to take this opportunity, before the resolution carries, of bringing to the attention of the house a matter which is one of some serious concern in British Columbia at this time. I may not have another suitable opportunity until we reach the details of the estimates of the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Labour and that may be some time.
I am referring to an investigation which is going on under the Combines Investigation Act into the activities of the fishermen's union of British Columbia. I might recall to the attention of the committee that on May 21, as recorded on page 4115 of Hansard of that date, I asked a question on the orders of the day of the Minister of Justice which was based upon a letter directed to the Minister of Labour, a copy of which I had received prior to asking that question. The Minister of Justice did make a statement which was related to the question arising out of section 4 of the Combines Investigation Act, which says:
Nothing in this act shall be construed to apply to combinations ol workmen or employees for their own reasonable protection as such workmen or employees.

The Minister of Justice went on to point out that the matter was before the courts in British Columbia, inasmuch as the fishermen's union had applied for an injunction restraining the investigation. However, this matter seems to continue to be carried forward and, as I say, is causing quite a bit of concern, particularly in trade union circles in British Columbia.
To point out on what that is based, it might be advisable if I were to draw the attention of the committee to a joint letter which was addressed to the Minister of Labour from the secretary treasurer of the B.C. federation of labour and the B.C. trade union congress, which two bodies are in process of merging as the British Columbia element of the new Canadian Labour Congress. They addressed this letter, dated June 1, to the Minister of Labour, and a copy of it was sent to me:
Dear Sir,
We wish to bring to your immediate attention the joint views of the B.C. Trade Union Congress, and the B.C. Federation of Labour, re the investigation now being conducted under the Combines Act into the affairs of the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union.
1.	It is our contention that use of the Combines Act in regard to said union, or any union, is in direct contravention of the original intent of the act.
2.	That, to preclude such use and abuse of the act, clause 4 was written into said act.
3.	It is the contention of labour in B.C., that as Minister of Labour, it is your duty to protect an}' union from such unjust investigation.
4.	Further, that the act will fall into disrepute, and will fail to fulfil its original intent if we allow it to become a weapon of persecution against the trade union movement to be instigated at the whim of any disgruntled or malicious minority.
5.	According to our information the action taken by the chairman of the restrictive trade practices commission in instituting this investigation was not mandatory upon him. That he, as a public servant, should take cognizance of the implications and ramifications of his action before instigating such an investigation against a union. That, while his action is unilateral in scope at present, and impinges only against the union, and one primary product, carried to its logical conclusion it would include all unions concerned in primary production, and agricultural production, thus involving all phases of the federal government's own grain prices, and agricultural products price support policy.
The letter concludes by urging the Minister of Labour to intercede on behalf of the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union. In this connection I must say that I was very much gratified to see what I considered a forthright statement from the Minister of Fisheries upon this subject, as quoted in The Fisherman, the union's newspaper, under date of May 22, 1956. They reprint in full a copy of a letter which was addressed to their organization by the

Minister of Fisheries. In the course of that letter the minister has this to say:
I . . . took it for granted that it (the union) would be excluded under section 4 of the Combines Act.
Perhaps I should report the statement of the minister a little more fully. In part of the letter, he says:
I must confess my own surprise that the method by which the fishing companies and your union negotiate minimum prices at the beginning of a fishing season should be regarded as price fixing within terms of the act. I had always regarded it as exactly similar to wage negotiations between other companies and unions, and understood that the procedure for such negotiations was provided for in the Fisheries Act of British Columbia. I seem to recall that the provincial minister of labour has on at least one occasion acted as mediator in these negotiations. I therefore took for granted that it would be excluded under section 4 which covers union agreements.
The reference to the fact that the minister of labour of British Columbia has acted as conciliator is, I believe, quite correct. Also I might point out that, according to the information I have received, there have been occasions when justices of the province of British Columbia had acted in the same role and that this whole matter, as far as we in British Columbia understand it, has been a well-established practice for a period of the past 20 years or so and has been carried on under the authority of the British Columbia fisheries act. Consequently I think it is very understandable that the central trade union bodies of British Columbia should be gravely concerned at the rather sudden launching of this investigation.
I know when the Minister of Justice replied on May 21-and I have referred to this earlier-he indicated he felt that it was mandatory, when a request was made under section 7 of the Combines Investigation Act, that an investigation should be instituted by the director. Section 7 of the act reads as follows:
Any six persons, Canadian citizens, resident in Canada, of the full age of 21 years, who are of the opinion that an offence has been or is being committed against section 32 or 34 of this act, or section 498 or 498A of the Criminal Code, chapter 36 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, may apply to the director for an inquiry into such matter, and shall place before the director the evidence on which such opinion is based.
Then subsection 2 goes on to explain that the application must be accompanied by a statement in the form of a statutory declaration. Then section 8 says:
The director shall
(a)	on application made under section 7-
Then it goes on to explain that the director can also do it on his own initiative or under the direction of the minister.

-cause an inquiry to be made into all such matters as he considers necessary to inquire into with the view of determining the facts.
It would appear from the way the act stands at the present time that certain action is mandatory as far as the director is concerned. But I would respectfully suggest that there is room for a good deal of discretion to be exercised by the director under the terms of section 8 of the act as to the type of inquiry that he initiates under certain conditions. It does seem to me that in view of the existence of section 4 of the act the director could very well have met the conditions required to be met by him under section 8 when he received an application made under section 7 by satisfying himself that the issue concerned was the proper activities carried on by a trade union in the protection of the workmen engaged in that industry, and that could have been done without taking the steps that have been taken in entering the union's premises and abstracting their documents and records.
It does seem to me that the union, in some of the correspondence they have sent to me and I think to a number of other members of the house, have made a good point when they state that their agreements made between themselves and the fishing companies of British Columbia are matters of public record, that they are on file with the . Department of Labour in Ottawa and also with the department of labour in Victoria, and that it should have been possible for the director to carry on an investigation which would have satisfied him that the union was in fact carrying on its normal activities as a union organization under the particular conditions prevailing in that industry, without having to go into a full-scale inquiry.
That may be a point that can be argued. As hon. members know, I am not one who is learned in the law, but I would submit on the basis of what has been happening that if it is mandatory upon the director under the present law to engage in the kind of inquiry into the activities of a trade union which has been made in these circumstances, serious consideration should be given to changing the law to provide the kind of protection that I believe was in mind when section 4 was written into the Combines Investigation Act. I think either that is the case, or the discretion exercised by the director of the Combines Investigation Act in approaching this problem is open to question.
As I explained at the outset, Mr. Chairman, because of the fact that I felt it might be some time before I could properly raise this question on the particular estimates of an

Mr. Chairman, this resolution offers an opportunity to draw the minister's attention to a certain action of his or rather lack of action which is causing considerable uncertainty and some unrest to a large and important segment of the business community of Canada. The situation has arisen in this way. On March 20, when the Minister of Finance brought down his budget, he announced the proposed imposition, provided the house would agree to it, of a 20 per cent tax on the advertising revenue of Canadian editions of United States magazines. Having made that announcement he took no further steps in that direction, and has consistently refused to give the house any indication as to when this legislation will be brought before us for discussion or when a final decision on it will be reached by the house.
Twice in the intervening months, and there have been three intervening months since then, from March 20 to April 20, from April 20 to May 20 and from May 20 to June 20, he has been questioned on the matter. The first time was on April 12, when he said he had received certain representations in connection with this legislation. He stated then, as found at page 2852 of Hansard:
All of these representations are of course being considered by the government and will be dealt with when we reach the resolution stage.
Just a few days ago, on June 15, the Minister of Finance would give no clear-cut indication as to when we would reach the resolution stage on his budget resolutions so we could deal with this particular item, and when he was asked about the 20 per cent tax he said, as found at page 5061 of Hansard:
I have made no announcement and would not do so until that time, sir.
It may seem to the minister and to the majority of the cabinet, who have been out of touch with the administration of a normal business operation for a good many years- in fact I doubt if some of them have ever been in touch with it-that when a decision is reached as to the imposition of a tax the point at which it is reached has no bearing on business plans whatsoever, provided that the tax is not imposed retroactively. My principal reason for rising this afternoon is to point out to the minister that in a case such as this uncertainties do arise from the time the tax is announced as a proposed imposition until it is finally endorsed by the house, if it is endorsed, and in that period 
there is great difficulty for business because of the uncertainty under which it must operate. I think the minister himself recognized that to some extent when he brought down his budget resolutions in their initial stage, because at that time he said with reference to this tax, as found at page 2334 of Hansard:
It will not come into eifect until January 1, 1957, so that those concerned may have time to adapt their affairs to it.
It is the final words in that sentence-"so that those concerned may have time to adapt their affairs to it"-which are important. At that point the minister gave some recognition to the fact that it is necessary to adjust one's affairs to certain types and levels of taxation. That is particularly so in a case such as this.
The minister should realize that while he may plan to impose his tax on January 1, 1957, that is not necessarily the time at which many business firms will make their decisions which are affected by the tax. Many organizations in this country establish an advertising budget period of one year, and they make their plans for the entire year in advance. In a great many cases that period starts in the fall. The result is that during the summer months-during the period in which we are now right through into August and September-corporations and advertising agencies and media suppliers across this country are all engaged in planning ahead. The media suppliers are engaged in selling their space. The advertisers and the agencies are engaged in deciding which media they will use, how much of each and in what form.
The tax to which I refer-without discussing its merits at this point, because that can better be done when the resolution is before this house-will have a great effect upon these particular plans. If it is to be a 20 per cent tax it is quite likely that the advertising rates of certain magazines will adjust themselves in accordance therewith. If, as is quite possible in view of the representations made to him and in view of the arguments made in the early days of April in this house, the minister is going to adjust his plans and reduce the tax or eliminate it completely, it will affect the entire advertising pattern of many of the major industries here in Canada.
At the moment, Mr. Chairman, all these organizations are completely unaware of what the government's plans may be. They know that the minister announced a 20 per cent tax on the advertising revenue of Canadian editions of American magazines. They also know that very strong, definite, well-substantiated and intelligent representations have been made to him, both in this house and

outside it, which might very well lead him to adjust that tax downward or to eliminate it entirely. They know that the minister has evaded and sidestepped any inquiries in this house as to what may be his course of action.
Frankly, I am glad to see him sidestep, because I think it may indicate that he is coming to his senses, and that he realizes that he was led part way down the garden path by those who suggested that this tax be imposed. But be that as it may, that uncertainty exists and is going to exist until such time as this house resolves, through its action, the course which the government will be empowered to take.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that it is unfair to the business of this country to expect it to continue for two, three or four months in a condition of uncertainty brought about through no other reason than the government's fumbling and stumbling, and its unawareness of the normal operating methods of the business community of Canada.
I feel that it is a wise thing and a good thing that following the announcement of a proposed taxation policy or budget there should be an interim period in which business organizations and all those others who are affected may have the opportunity to make representations to the minister. I suggest that a normal period of that type might be some two or three weeks. But if within that period those organizations have not come forward and made their representations, I for one am not prepared to worry too much about them. It is their responsibility to get up here to Ottawa with great rapidity once they know the taxation pattern of the government, and to present their views on the subject to the government and to whatever members of this house they may wish to select.
Then it is the government's responsibility to examine those views. Then-and rapidly -it is the government's responsibility to bring to this house their definite final conclusions, to offer this house the opportunity to debate them, and to facilitate this house passing either the government's proposals or whatever amendments may be made to them by the house into the law of the country so that business knows where it stands.
As to this type of situation, I have picked out one specific instance, namely the advertising tax, because I am reasonably familiar with that field and because I know the uncertainties which the lack of action of the government are causing. This type of uncertainty seems to exist continuously in a great many fields as a result of announcing activities and then letting them hang around indefinitely.
Interim Supply
As has been suggested many times, I think you must get your legislative pattern into the books early in the year. Some of it is going to have to be delayed. We admit that. But in the case of the budget, the thing that strikes right at the very vitals of the business economy of this country, I think it is the responsibility of the minister to stop horsing around, to stop living in his ivory tower so far removed from the everyday realities of the business man who must eventually pay his taxes, and to try to understand in some small way the difficulties which he is unnecessarily putting in the path of business in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to use this opportunity afforded by the introduction of the interim supply resolution to bring a matter to the attention of the government. I had anticipated bringing this subject up at a later period for discussion, particularly under the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. It seems, however, that discussion of this department's affairs might be delayed somewhat, and I feel the subject is of sufficient urgency to merit the immediate consideration of the government.
It does not concern the subject of the rights of parliament, which was raised earlier in the discussion today. It does, however, concern the matter of the rights of a private citizen, who happens to be living in my constituency. The name of the gentleman concerned is August Fontana, who until the year 1940 operated a farm near the town of Virden in the province of Manitoba. Mr. Fontana was an immigrant from Italy to Canada, in the latter part of the last century. He became a naturalized citizen in 1903. After much hard work and careful saving, he was able to gather together sufficient money to purchase a half section of land in the Virden area. As I have indicated, he worked that land as a farm until the year 1940. During the period he established a solid reputation for himself and the members of his family in the district. Altogether 10 children were born to Mr. and Mrs. Fontana, seven of whom still survive.
Now, it has been brought to my attention, as it has been to the attention of other hon. members of the house, that a grave injustice has been done to this particular individual either by accident or by intent. I feel sincerely it deserves the attention of the ministers of the crown at this time. Around about August 20, 1940, I believe Mr. Fontana was approached by one named Clifford Johnston, who at that time was a land inspector for the Canadian National Railways. I believe

Interim Supply
Mr. Johnston was representing the Department of Transport and was canvassing Mr. Fontana to see if that gentleman would be willing to turn his farm over for use as an airfield under the commonwealth air training plan. Expropriation action, I understand, was taken; but before that proceeded Mr. Fontana, being a loyal and responsible Canadian, was quite happy to transfer the land for the patriotic purpose of making possible the establishment of an airfield in this particular area. The transfer procedure took place. The necessary deeds were registered in the land titles office of the town of Virden. Shortly after the Fontana farm became an elementary flying school under the commonwealth air training plan.
The difficulty concerning this transaction has arisen over the mineral rights. There was no specific mention of expropriating or transferring the mineral rights under the action that was necessary in transferring these lands to the crown. I find Mr. Fontana made no specific reference to the mineral rights. However, Mr. Johnston, the agent who represented the crown, as indicated in the petition that has come into the hands of all hon. members, specified that he definitely informed Mr. Fontana that the government would not be requiring the mineral rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Oh, no.

They were interested only in the surface rights, and that of course is obvious because the land was to be used for an airport and the mineral rights had no specific function in the operation of the property as an airport.
At the time Mr. Fontana had been taking gravel from the farm, and he received permission to continue the removal of certain quantities of gravel from the property that had been formerly his. Gravel, of course, is classified as a mineral in Manitoba. The total price for the transaction was $9,000, and that represents $28 per acre. This was the going price for farm land in August of 1940. The price certainly does not include any compensation for the mineral rights.
In August, 1954, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources inserted an advertisement in the Virden Empire-Advance, as well as in other newspapers, inviting tenders for the purchase of a lease of the petroleum and natural gas rights which underlie this particular parcel of land under discussion here this afternoon. Several offers were received. One was an offer of $200,000 in cash, a royalty of 12-5 per cent and an annual rental of $1 per acre per year. Now, that is a fairly substantial return for the $9,000 invested, and by that action the government was indicating it was no longer

interested in any claim that Mr. Fontana had as the former owner of this parcel of land. Mr. Fontana's legal advisers immediately placed a caveat against the land and there, I believe, is where the matter stands at the moment.
The legal advisers also commenced proceedings in the Exchequer Court of Canada. According to the petition that has come into our hands, an approach was made to the Exchequer Court of Canada on February 8, 1954, alleging:
(a)	That your petitioner was never compensated in any way for the alleged loss of his minerals;
(b) That it was not the intention of your petitioner to part with, nor the intention of the crown to acquire the mines and minerals;
(c)	That in the result the crown was being unjustly enriched at the expense of your petitioner;
(d)	That the crown should be declared to be a trustee of the mines and minerals.
The petition goes on to say further:
That the crown immediately launched a motion in court to strike out the petition on the ground that it was frivolous, vexatious and an abuse of the court's process, and the crown succeeded in that motion. A subsequent appeal by your petitioner to the Supreme Court of Canada met a like fate.
I want to emphasize the point that the merits of the case were never discussed, merely the motion that Mr. Fontana's appeal to the courts was frivolous, vexatious and an abuse of the court's process. There has never been any court hearing on the merits of this particular case. I think that is very important in view of the events that have transpired since that time.
Section 24 of the Expropriation Act, chapter 64 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, says:
Whenever, from time to time, or at any time before the compensation money has been actually paid, any parcel of land taken for a public work, or any portion of such parcel, is found to be unnecessary for the purposes of such public work, or if it is found that a more limited estate or interest therein only is required, the minister may, by writing under his hand, declare that the land or such portion thereof is not required and is abandoned by the crown, or that it is intended to retain only such limited estate or interest as is mentioned in such writing.
Subsection 2 of section 24 reads:
Upon such writing being registered in the office of the registrar of deeds for the county or registration division in which the land is situate, such land declared to be abandoned shall revest in the person from whom it was taken or in those entitled to claim under him.
Subsection 3 of section 24 reads:
In the event of a limited estate or interest therein being retained by the crown, the land shall so revest subject to the estate or interest so retained.

Subsection 4 of section 24 reads:
The fact of such abandonment or revesting shall be taken into account, in connection with all the other circumstances of the case, in estimating or assessing the amount to be paid to any person claiming compensation for the land taken.
Under the Canadian expropriation law it is clearly stated that Mr. Fontana has a definite claim of continued interest in this land which was expropriated for war purposes. The petitioner has made his appeal to what we might call the last court of appeal, the parliament of Canada, which seeks to protect the rights of the individual citizen. Because he has been frustrated in seeking recourse through legal channels he has brought his petition to the House of Commons.
There is a precedent for this type of case in the mother of parliaments at Westminster in the famous Crichel Down case. It was written up in book form and has become somewhat of a classic. The Crichel Down case arose out of certain expropriation actions that took place in the old country in order to meet the demands of war.
As a result of Mr. Down's appeal to parliament the land which had been taken to establish a bombing range was revested in the original owner. It had been kicked around by government officials for some considerable time and had been removed entirely from any claim of ownership by the farmer, Mr. Down, and had been made into a solid parcel of land operated by the land ministry. Mr. Down brought his appeal to the House of Commons at Westminster through his member. There was a public inquiry, and as a result of that inquiry he received once again complete ownership of the land. I understand the minister concerned found it necessary to resign because of the nature of the proceedings that had taken place that had deprived Mr. Down of his normal claim to this property.
In the debate on the subject in the British House of Commons which took place on July 20, 1954, as recorded at page 1296 of the British Hansard, Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe said:
Every citizen of good will will see his land go in time of emergency for government requirements with as much good will as he can muster-
Certainly that applies to Mr. Fontana, a Canadian citizen of Italian descent, who in every respect has made an outstanding contribution to this country and to his community. When he was approached by Mr. Johnston there was no hesitancy at all in his letting the land go to meet the exigency of war. Continuing with Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe's remarks:
-but it is taken for a specific purpose, for a specific need of the state. When that purpose Is
Interim Supply
exhausted, when that need is past, what is wrong, on any consideration of morality or justice, in allowing the person from whom the land was taken to have the chance of getting it back.
In the Crichel Down case only surface rights were concerned, and the surface rights were revested in the original owner. Mr. Fontana is not interested in the surface rights. The town of Virden is operating this particular piece of property as a flying club at the moment, and the crown is renting the property for that purpose. Despite the fact it is operated as a flying club only the mineral rights are involved. There has never been any specific need for the crown to usurp the mineral rights, which would still be in Mr. Fontana's possession had there been no war and had Mr. Fontana not been forced to turn over the land for the war emergency by the threat of expropriation proceedings.
I am not making this appeal from the standpoint of legal rights. I am making this appeal from the standpoint of very deep and sincere moral obligation. There is a genuine moral obligation involved in this case. The crown is receiving an advantage that was never intended and for which Mr. Fontana was never compensated in any shape or form. I suggest to this committee, Mr. Chairman, that is a violation of the rights of a private citizen of Canada. Revestment of the surface rights of the land is not possible, but under section 24 of the Expropriation Act reconveyance of the mineral rights is certainly quite possible. It is within the power of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to undertake that reconveyance, and certainly it is within the power of the government to compensate this very worthy Canadian citizen for the wrong which has been done.
All he has ever asked for in any action taken is that he be restored to a position of equality with his neighbours who were not asked to give up their land for the purposes of establishing an airport, and who are today enjoying all the rights and privileges and advantages of owning land in an area which has become a rich oil-bearing area. He is merely asking for simple justice, equality with his neighbours. He could have been enjoying that equality, he could have been enjoying that right had he not been sufficiently patriotic to yield to the demands of the emergency back in 1940.
I do not know whether this matter has ever been considered in cabinet council, but it seems to me that it is a case deserving of such consideration. If there is any sense of moral obligation, if there is any sense of justice, then this case demands the urgent attention of the ministers of the crown. Failing that, then, as was done in Crichel Downs

Interim Supply
case in the old country, this citizen as a free citizen of Canada deserves the privilege of having the merits of his case presented at a public hearing.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to support the request made to the committee by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. At the outset perhaps I should say that unlike the hon. member I am not personally acquainted with the party concerned. He does not live in my constituency, but there is a principle involved which I think goes much further than any individual case. I think it is from that point of view that my colleague, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, approaches this matter.
I note from the petition he quoted that the gentleman to whom he has referred, Mr. Fontana, came to Canada at the age of 21 and settled near Virden, Manitoba, some number of years ago. As was the case with many other immigrants who arrived in Canada years ago and were of more or less adult age, he did not have the opportunity or the free time to become educated. In many cases it was difficult for these people to even learn to read or write. That may not seem like a strong argument for what I am about to say, but it is something which those of us who have had the advantage of learning, the advantage of getting some sort of education, should always bear in mind. There are many thousands of people in this country who have made a great contribution to this nation through their work, through their production, and because of the families they have raised, who did not have the advantages which were open to those of us who were younger. That is one reason we as representatives in this parliament of the people generally should give a sympathetic ear when some person in that category feels that injustice is being done.
On June 12 last I addressed a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources with regard to this matter, and then on the following day I wrote a letter to him setting out some of the considerations with regard to this case. I am glad the opportunity has now arisen to place the matter before members of this house in a more formal manner.
It seems quite clear from a reading of the petition which was sent to most members, and of the copy of the resolution passed at a public meeting on April 21 this year, and of the letter which accompanied the petition written by Mr. Riley, who apparently was acting for Mr. Fontana, that several things stand out. First is the fact that the land was required for the purpose of an airport. The government was not desirous of acquiring a piece of land for the purpose of speculation
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
or with any thought of making a profit from the transaction. It was during an emergency when the government approached this farmer and asked him for the use of his land for war purposes, of course with compensation. For that reason alone I think it is quite clear that there was no intention on the part of the government to acquire anything more than surface rights and those for a specific purpose for a specific length of time, for the duration of the war.
Second, the compensation paid is clear indication that any other values or rights than the use of the surface of this half section were not a consideration. I was not in the real estate business in 1940, but I have been in it for quite a number of years since. I am thoroughly familiar with land values, not only in my own part of the province but in the area concerned. Certainly no one could argue that a half section of land in the vicinity of Virden which was sold for a consideration of $9,000 was being sold for anything but the surface use. It was not an excessive price; in my opinion it was quite a moderate price.
Third, it is now clear that by fortuitous circumstances the government stand to gain approximately $200,000 or some larger undetermined amount if they go ahead and accept the offer which has been made by an oil company, for which they paid no compensation. It could amount to a great deal more than that, but in any event it is in the vicinity of $200,000.
With these facts before us I think this committee should give consideration to the petition which has been presented. There is also the fact that the gentleman to whom the hon. member for Brandon-Souris referred, Mr. Johnston, who apparently acted for the crown in negotiating this purchase, wrote a letter dated December 6, 1955 addressed to D. O. Owens, Q.C., regional counsel, Canadian National Railways, Winnipeg, Manitoba, which I think should be placed on the record so we may know what we are referring to. The letter reads:
Dear Sir:
W 1/2 35-10-26-W 1st-Virden Airfield August Fontana
I have read over the petition being presented on behalf of August Fontana in connection with the purchase of the above mentioned acreage in 1940 by the crown for airfield purposes; also statutory declarations by Jack Fontana, August Fontana and Deno Fontana, and to the best of my recollection believe the statements to be true.
I pause there for a moment to point out that he makes the definite statement that after carefully examining the statements made in the petition and the declarations accompanying it he believes those statements

to be true. He was the one most intimately concerned in these negotiations. I continue:
At that time mineral rights were not considered of any particular value and were not a factor in arriving at a valuation for the acreage. Some mention was made of sand and gravel and, to the best of my recollection, Mr. Fontana had promised delivery of some sand or gravel and it was suggested he had better remove same before acceptance of his offer to sell by the crown.
Yours truly,
C. Johnston.
The important parts of that letter, in my opinion, are the ones I have already mentioned; that in his opinion the statements contained in the petition are true and, second, that at the time of arriving at a valuation of the land, mineral rights were not considered. Under those circumstances the gentleman who represented the crown in the negotiations is giving us primary evidence that the mineral rights were not a consideration and therefore, of course, no compensation was paid for them in that sense.
I suppose the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources could argue as a lawyer that since Mr. Fontana signed an agreement under which he surrendered his interests in that parcel of land, even without any specific mention of mineral rights, by doing so he gave up all his interest in that land. I am not going into a long argument on the legal aspects of that position.
He could probably also argue that the courts would agree with his view. Apparently the courts have ruled that the claim should not be received, but I would point out that the reason this claim comes before this committee at all is that there is something much more than the legal considerations involved. Even if the minister were to argue that this has been before the courts and the courts have ruled that the gentleman in question has no claim, may I remind him that that has not always been the end of the line. Not so long ago on two occasions in this house I had to question the actions of the government in making certain remissions of taxation to certain corporations in the province of Quebec after the exchequer court had ruled that those remissions should not be made. In the wisdom or otherwise of the cabinet, the government decided otherwise. In fact they argued that there were other considerations than the strictly legal ones involved.
I should certainly think that, if the government is willing to make a concession to wealthy corporations, which after all are not in any great need of these tax remissions that run collectively in the neighbourhood of $6 million, then in the case of a family that has contributed to the welfare of this country, the gentleman himself being now 86
Interim Supply
years of age, desirous of leaving a little nest egg for those who are inheriting his property when he passes on, certainly the government could lean over to the side of generosity. I am sure there would not be a word of criticism from anyone in this committee nor from anyone in the country if they were to pay that amount, even if the legality of the claim is in doubt. There is a moral obligation on the part of the crown to compensate the man who was the owner of these valuable mineral rights with which he parted without his knowledge.
If the feelings in the community of Virden, where after all the people are best acquainted with the circumstances and with the gentleman concerned, are any indication of how it would be taken by the public generally, I think the government has a clear duty to give sympathetic and favourable consideration to this petition. Perhaps it would be wise to place on the record also a resolution that was passed on April 21, 1956, in Legion Hall, Virden, Manitoba, by the citizens of that community. I might note that this was unanimously passed at this public gathering. Here is the text of that resolution:
Whereas the west half section 35-10-26-Wlst, Manitoba, was during the fall of 1940 expropriated by the government of Canada for an airport (or purchased under threat of compulsion) from August Fontana under circumstances in which It is now clear that the mineral rights underlying the same were never bought, were never intended to be bought, and were never paid for, and the said Fontana remains and is the true owner thereof notwithstanding that by a mistake or accident or inadvertence in the conveyancing the title to the said mineral rights became vested in the crown in the right of the Dominion of Canada.
And whereas it also now appears that the said government of Canada proposes to retain and maintain the said airport for future purposes and that in order to do so the development and operation of underlying minerals may be carried out without interfering in any way with the operation of the said airport in accordance with the regulations pertaining to the same.
Now therefore we, the citizens and ratepayers of Manitoba, having heard the situation and the history of this case fully explained in a public meeting and being convinced beyond all question that the said August Fontana is the true owner of the said mineral rights and being desirous of expressing to the government as such citizens, that we would greatly deplore any action or lack of action by the said government that would deprive the said Fontana of his just rights:
We do hereby petition and request the said government and the minister having jurisdiction in the matter, that the said mineral rights be restored to said August Fontana and that advantage be taken of the provisions of the Expropriation Act, being chapter 64 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, which applied at the time of the said expropriation, and particularly section 24 thereof, and that the same be invoked to do justice to the said Fontana and to enable him to receive back the title to the said mineral rights.
Respectfully submitted

Interim Supply
It is signed by the chairman and secretary of the meeting. On the basis of the strict wording contained in this resolution I can immediately see a few loopholes, in that the minister might be tempted to point out that certain statements are made which are not supported in the resolution itself by any evidence. But, apart altogether from that, in view of the fact that the government, without going out deliberately to make a property purchase which involved the rights of mineral exploitation, happened to receive a piece of property which contains those mineral rights and were in line to benefit to the extent of about $200,000, what would be wrong with this parliament giving consideration to this request?
If the government feels that it cannot go the whole way and cannot revest the rights in the original owner, then perhaps it could suggest a compromise. I am sure those who are concerned are reasonable people and would be willing to give consideration to any reasonable proposal, but certainly the government should not simply slam the door in the face of a citizen and say, "Because, on a strictly technical and legal basis, you signed an agreement by virtue of which you signed away the interest in your property, then we have nothing more to consider," and turn their back on his claims. I think that would be morally wrong, and it would be setting a very bad example.
I think this is a case where the government would be very well advised to lean to the side of generosity. As I said at the beginning, there is a principle involved. This is not the only person in the province of Manitoba, or probably in Canada, who may be faced in the future with a similar situation. I know there will not be a large number of such cases, or we hope there will not, but there will be other cases. I hope the government, by turning down this case, by shutting the door and turning their back, will not say they have created a precedent upon which they cannot go back. I hope when the next one comes along they will not say, "We could not do it for Mr. Fontana; therefore we cannot do it for you." Let us start off on the right foot this time. Let us do something for a worthy cause, and then we will leave the door open for the future to give sympathetic consideration if and when the situation arises.

Mr. Chairman,
I might say that this is very much like coming to bat in every inning so far as this debate is concerned, and I would say that even if I take my full time I will still have another inning coming to me. Therefore it will be very difficult for me to carry on with, shall I say, any follow-through in connection with the remarks I started last night.
Perhaps, however, I might be allowed to summarize some of the things I said at that time. I said first of all that I was somewhat surprised that so little concern was shown on the other side of the house about an expenditure of $1,775 million. I also referred to the extreme interest that was shown during the pipe-line debate by all parties, by the galleries and by the press, when we were discussing an expenditure of only about $200 million. I think I also said that the government indicated that they hoped to get it all back. I said that up until that time yesterday, however, we had had a speech from only one other member of the government outside of the minister. As I was saying that I heard a remark in the distance "Give us a chance".
Mr. Chairman, those gentlemen are going to get the chance, but I wonder just what their interest is in this matter. When they get the chance-and I am assuming they are going to wait for the detailed estimates-I wonder whether they are going to tell us about some article like the coat of arms that needs replacing in the armoury at Podunk Centre or some place like that, or whether they are really interested in a complete and over-all defence policy which must be laid down sooner or later by this government.
I said-and I repeat it-that it was most difficult for us over here to break through and get the information we required. The chief reason was that it is a very illusory opponent with whom we must grapple. I said as well-and General Simonds referred to this matter-that there is a hard crust of experts who surround the minister and who are responsible for bringing in each year the items which are mentioned in this book. I think I should mention again that there is every appearance that the formula used is to arrive at a total figure which the government think they can get through the house, and then work back from the bottom of their

Supply-National Defence work sheet to the top and reconcile the individual items with that total amount.
Yesterday, Mr. Chairman, I quoted one example, and I recall that after I had spoken one of the members from the Waterloo area said to me, "That is the way business must be done; this is only an estimate of what we are going to use for this year". Mr. Chairman, how can we honestly back up an estimate-at a time when we are talking about hundreds of millions of dollars-when the estimate comes out each time almost identical in amount with that which was spent in the previous year? I referred the other day to a specific item in these estimates-I think it is to be found at page 337-dealing with the repair of aircraft engines, where the total amount is approximately $119 million. I found that the sharp pencils this year have come practically to the same conclusion, dollarwise, as they came to last year; the amount of the estimate is practically the same. It seems to me that these are things that should be examined by a committee qualified to do that particular type of work.
Since I last spoke the Prime Minister has been on his feet. He is going away to a commonwealth conference. He was asked by my leader what commitments he could make to the house before he left on the calling of a defence committee here to review these expenditures. I think these are the answers he gave. He said this was not going to be possible because our constitution is quite different from the constitution in the United States, where such a committee is used. He said that all the expenditures in connection with the carrying out of the work of our armed forces in this country are recommended by the governor general. Then he said that in the United States the policy is to have these recommendations come from an estimates committee of the two houses.
Surely those are not adequate reasons for refusing to constitute a committee which for the first time could look behind the large and generous amounts that are set aside for this purpose. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that we are going along a road that has no turning. Up to this point we have never been allowed to get the information which the Canadian public deserves in connection with these amounts. If we approach too close to forbidden territory we are told by the minister that this is classified material, that this is an amount which cannot be discussed further because it will not be in the public interest to do so. Yet as I said last year, and I say it again this year, in connection with some of the information and in fact practically all the information that we are refused in this house, you can wait six or


seven months and, if you follow the course of the news magazines, you can find the very answers that have been refused to us on the floor of the house.
Surely there is no longer reason to refuse us. the actual unit cost of an aircraft or the actual unit cost of an engine for an aircraft. Surely there is no longer reason to refuse us the comparative figures in connection with what is paid for an article of that kind in this country and what is paid for an article of a similar nature in another country. Surely there is no reason for not giving us exact figures on the number of aircraft which have been produced. As a matter of fact, as I recall it, in connection with the CF-100 we were unable to get specific figures on the production schedule or the number of planes which have been produced. Yet the other day I read in the Montreal Gazette a complete breakdown showing how many planes had been produced. We can tie that information in, then, with the number that are operational.
When I think of the remarks made by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace last night I am wondering whether this refusal to give this information was not because of a dancing class mentality. That dancing class mentality is one which permits the expenditure of money for items which are not in fact contributing to the carrying out of an over-all defence policy, while at the same time we may be skimping on other items of an urgent nature.
I think the government must take the blame for the situation in which we find ourselves.
I believe the people have reached the point where they feel that large expenditures of money on this type of equipment have in fact brought them along the road toward the achievement of a high standard of living, and they may be reluctant to turn back and examine them in detail. I believe that feeling has been enhanced, has been furthered, by the government; and behind it and keeping it high is a group who perhaps got their basic training during the period of depression, when one of their main objectives was to ensure that every article they could possibly squeeze out would be obtained for the particular branch of the forces they represented. As a matter of fact, at that time it may have been a very laudable effort on their part, but now that it has been carried forward into this period of inflation it may, in fact, cost us millions of dollars which are not required.
I wonder, sir, if at this time we can just take for granted everything which is set out in the white paper. It seems to me that a halt must be called at some stage, and we must ask the minister to back up the

statements which are contained in this booklet. Surely parliament is entitled to some proof of the background that goes into the making up of this annual statement. I find it difficult to understand how the Prime Minister can go away at this time, with no commitments as to the calling of a committee such as has been suggested by my leader, in the face of these charges which have been published in various periodicals by the ex-chief of the general staff.
As I said yesterday, we do not have to say that these statements are true in order to call for the forming of that committee. Here is one man who should have known what the situation was and is in connection with our armed forces. Here is the only outside evidence that to date we in the opposition can look to as indicating what may be wrong in our armed forces. Yet the Prime Minister can say there are two or three differences between the system we have and the system in the United States which preclude the opposition from benefiting from the evidence of experts such as these.
Let us not make any mistake about it. While I was talking here last night we were having distributed about 250,000 copies of the Toronto Evening Telegram. In that newspaper there is almost a full page story by the retiring adjutant general on the sad state of the militia. Here is a second potent condemnation of the policy of this government in connection with defence matters.
I said last night that I would have preferred, sir, if the matters of principle which are set out in these articles had been great enough to the gentleman in question to mention during their tenure of office. Even though I may feel that way, that does not mean these conditions do not exist. Perhaps these same men-and we will be anxiously awaiting an answer from the minister-have made recommendations as set out here and their wishes have not been followed. We shall never know the truth or falsehood of those allegations without the committee that has been suggested. I am only going to refer to them very briefly, but I think they should be recorded in Hansard in the short form in which they appear in the Maclean's magazine article by Lieutenant General Simonds. I think they might be recorded point by point:
1.	There is no co-ordinated effort to evolve a sound and comprehensive defence policy.
2.	The Canadian chiefs of staff committee is "packed" to protect the government against the receipt of unpalatable advice.
3.	Senior civil servants can, by deliberate and unwarranted stalling, defeat the recommendations of the armed forces even though those recommendations have been approved by the cabinet.
4.	The . . . chiefs of the three armed services are denied an opportunity to confront those responsible for political decisions with objective military advice.
Private Bills
5.	Certain politicians . . . have raised the bogey
of a so-called military "junta" attempting to usurp political powers. Such fantasies .	.	.
represent one of the most outrageous hoaxes ever inflicted upon an unsuspecting public and Canadian political twisting at its worst and most degrading.
6.	There is no facet of our national affairs in which the stamp of a colonial mentality remains so deeply embedded as in that of our national defence.
These charges are going to require a lot of explaining. It seems to me, sir, that on this occasion we will require primary evidence, not hearsay. It will no longer be possible to get by on the production of a certificate signed by the minister.
May I call it five o'clock?
Progress reported.
