speakeroldname: Mr. W. L. Houck (Niagara Falls) moved
maintopic: NIAGARA LOWER ARCH BRIDGE COMPANY LIMITED
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 434, respecting the Niagara Lower Arch Bridge Company Limited.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, there are two
important reasons why this bill is being brought before this honourable house, and I pray the indulgence of the house to make a brief explanation of the bill itself and to give a short outline of the history of the bridge.
This act respecting the Niagara Lower Arch Bridge Company Limited is similar to an act respecting the Detroit and Windsor Subway Company, which was passed through this house in February, 1953.
This federal act is necessary because the bridge is international, and simply corrects a technicality in the company's charter. The import of this bill is that the company is authorized and empowered to sell, assign, transfer and convey to any company, body or commission its bridge, the approaches thereto, all appurtenant structures, works, undertakings, franchises, privileges, powers, rights and property, real, personal, and mixed so far as the same are located within Canada, possessed by, vested in or to it belonging or heretofore possessed by vested in or belonging to The Niagara Falls Suspension Bridge Company. However, may I state that any assignment, transfer or conveyance must first be approved by the holders of two-thirds of the shares at a special general meeting of the shareholders, duly called for the purpose of considering this sale.
Although there is no question as to the validity of the company's title to its undertaking, doubts have arisen as to its power to convey its undertaking, and more particularly to convey its franchise to operate a bridge and collect tolls thereon. Naturally, the purpose of this proposed act is to remove any such doubts.
I would now like to say a few words about the history of the bridge. In 1844 the Hon. William Hamilton Merritt of St. Catharines, who was one of the builders of the original Welland canal, conceived the idea of bridging the Niagara river near the falls. In the year 1846 an act of parliament of the province of Canada was passed incorporating the Niagara Falls Suspension Bridge Company. There were ten original petitioners for incorporation. In the same year the Niagara Falls Suspension Bridge Company was incorporated by special act of the legislature of the state of New York. By 1848 a wooden bridge was in operation across the river.	,

About this time railway building was becoming very active in southern Ontario. By a special act the company was given certain rights to erect a railway bridge. In 1853, the rights granted under the act having been allowed to lapse, a further act was passed increasing the capitalization of the company to provide for the erection of a steel bridge capable of carrying a railway. The new bridge was finally built, and certain agreements between the Canadian and American bridge companies and the Great Western Railway Company were entered into and were confirmed in 1875 by an act of the parliament of the Dominion of Canada.
By 1894 trains had increased in size and weight and it was found necessary to make extensive structural alterations to the bridge. In order to finance this, yet another act was passed authorizing the issue of bonds and debentures. In 1919 further extensive work was done on the bridge structure, but this time no legislation was needed. In 1929 the bridge company was reincorporated under the provisions of the first part of the Companies Act.
The bridge company pays it full share of municipal taxes to the city of Niagara Falls, Ontario. It is interesting to note that this bridge has been in continuous operation longer than any other international bridge in the world. Traffic has crossed the Niagara river on this bridge without interruption since it was opened in 1848, except for a few hours in 1948 during the celebration of the centennial. I am sure the Leader of the Opposition will recall that day very vividly because he and the governor of New York state were the guest speakers on that occasion.
Some time ago, Mr. Speaker, the directors of the company were approached with respect to the sale of the bridge, but nothing resulted from this approach. At about that time counsel was instructed to consider the question of whether or not the company could sell or transfer its undertaking and especially its franchise to operate the bridge and to collect tolls. Counsel was of the opinion that in works, such as the bridge, in which the public have an interest, the corporation cannot delegate its powers or in any way divest itself of the obligation placed upon it by the legislature, except by express sanction of such legislature.
Someone might well ask about the capital of this company, and I just wish to state that it is divided into 15,000 shares, 7 per cent of which are held in the United States, 12 per cent in England, and the remaining 81 per cent in Canada. This stock is not listed on any exchange but it is traded on the
Supply-National Defence unlisted market. This bill has passed the Senate and will of course go to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are just one or two observations I should like to make with regard to the estimates now before the committee, which have to do in general with the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition that having regard to the tremendous amount being expended for defence, which during the year will total some $1,775 million, a closer and more meticulous examination should be made of the defence expenditures than can be achieved through the medium of the committee of supply.
I was surprised today to hear the Prime Minister dismiss the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition for the setting up of such a committee on the grounds that our system is different from that of the United States. I can see no merit in the excuse advanced

Supply-National Defence by the Prime Minister. These estimates are for a tremendous amount, and they cannot be given that examination which is necessary in committee of supply. This committee denies the calling of witnesses, and certainly there is springing up in our country a very strong feeling that in respect of the vast amounts being spent for defence, corresponding value is not being secured for the people of Canada. Only this evening there is an editorial in the Ottawa Journal which pretty well summarizes the situation. It is entitled "Too Little at Too Much Cost?"
I can see no reason why there should not be a careful examination; why these generals who enjoyed the respect of the government for so long and who are now freed from their shackles of silence should not be given the opportunity of appearing before a committee and being examined and cross-examined on their statements with a view to ascertaining whether or not there is foundation for their criticism. That to me would seem to be the logical course to follow, unless it is the desire of the minister and the government to conceal as far as possible the results being achieved by the expenditure of such vast amounts of money.
Indeed it is not so long ago that I saw figures which indicated that the cost of recruiting and training servicemen for the Canadian army was five times the cost in the United States per man, and even a greater number of times the cost of recruiting and training British servicemen. If that is the fact, and I think it is, there should be an examination to ascertain why. Laymen see expenditures being made for recruiting purposes in Canada, and the cost of advertising in order to secure recruits seems far beyond the needs of the moment if the government's attitude as revealed by the minister is to be taken as indicative of the present world situation. These and other matters deserve to be looked into and examined.
Mention was made by the minister of our responsibility to the NATO countries as one of the members of that great organization for peace. However, what do we know as a House of Commons of the attitude taken by NATO respecting the present world situation? What is the reason for the change of direction as announced by the minister, in that to a greater extent than ever before the emphasis will be on air troops and air facilities? These are questions that deserve examination.
What is the attitude of the Department of National Defence toward those nations that are doing their part to preserve our freedom in other parts of the world? What about the position today of Israel, standing in the Middle East with one or two others having a similar viewpoint toward democracy and


freedom? Recently the consensus of opinion has been that Colonel Nasser no longer holds toward the free nations the friendly attitude that one would expect from the leader of a country that owes so much to Britain.
What attitude is the government going to take toward the calls for help on the part of Israel, for assistance in the form of jet aircraft? A few months agcy there was uncertainty in regard to the attitude of Colonel Nasser toward the free world. Today, as we watch his activities from the shores of the Atlantic and thence through Iraq and Iran, this man shows more and more an attitude of disregard for the forces of freedom. Indeed, it would appear as though he had in mind the achievement by himself of an overlordship over all that area.
I ask these questions because they are material to our defences here in Canada. They are part and parcel of the problem of freedom being preserved in all parts of the world. Has the government as yet made a decision on the question of permitting the export of aircraft to Israel-not aircraft for the offensive, not bombers, but fighting aircraft whose business it would be to prevent, or at least to meet, any bombing attacks that might be made as against the state of Israel?
There in the Far East the situation is serious. Egypt has received colossal supplies of war material from the U.S.S.R. The man who negotiated the arrangements is the new foreign minister of the U.S.S.R., Dmitri Shepilov. He it was, who negotiated that nefarious agreement between Hitler and the U.S.S.R. in 1939. I ask the minister what is the attitude of the government to this problem, which becomes more pressing as days go by.
The Middle East is indeed the lifeline of the British commonwealth, and certainly of Great Britain herself. That area controls some 70 per cent of all the oil in the free world. Are we not now, in the light of the events that have taken place since January and February, in Canada called upon to do our part by way of assistance to Israel, to permit Israel as a bastion of defence in the Middle East to resist any aggression that may take place against her? That is a problem on which there should be information. It is one that is of challenging import to the preservation of freedom in that part of the world.
As I read the remarks of the Minister of National Defence, he glosses over the world situation. He warns here in one paragraph; he wavers slightly in another. In the light of the revelations that were made in the speech delivered about a week ago by Khrushchev during the visit of Tito to the U.S.S.R., following which there have been declarations

between Yugoslavia and the U.S.S.R. that, to say the least, are not indicative of a peaceful attitude, what has been achieved in recent months by the turnabout in attitude by the leaders of the U.S.S.R.? Would the minister enlighten the house and the country as to the attitude of the government on the recent denunciation of Stalin by Khrushchev?
Has the world situation not been deteriorating in recent weeks? Are the forces of freedom not, in recent weeks, once more meeting a very serious challenge brought about by the deceptive propaganda of the U.S.S.R.? I have read that speech of Khrushchev, as the minister has. It contains 27,000 words, a saga of the assassination of Stalin, wherein he is described as a murderer, a mass jailer of free peoples, a torturer, an enemy of freedom, an executioner without trial, and a destroyer of oppositions. It is a dangerous thing to be a member of an opposition in the U.S.S.R., for it is revealed by Khrushchev that of the 139 members of the seventeenth people's congress of 1940, 98 were shot.
This speech by Khrushchev is a testament of tyranny and a catalogue of cruelty, designed apparently to delude the free world. One of the statements that clarifies the atmosphere is that the trouble with Stalin was that he used terror at the wrong times against the wrong people. Then in another place he said that Lenin only resorted ruthlessly to the most extreme methods in the most necessary cases.
Is there a change of front? What attitude will Canada take as one of the free nations to meet the economic challenge of the U.S.S.R. everywhere in the world? Is there to be a reassessment on the part of Canada and the other free nations respecting the amount to be devoted to defence as such and the amount to be devoted as defence by way of economic policies designed to offset or meet the challenge of the U.S.S.R.? We have none of that information. What attitude are the NATO nations to take to the mass challenge all over the world of the U.S.S.R. in trade?
In the United States expenditures for aid and the like as part of the general defence picture were reduced by congress by approximately 20 per cent against the wishes of the President and his advisers. What is Canada going to do along with the other NATO nations to meet the penetration in underdeveloped lands of the U.S.S.R., as she offers to trade capital goods for surplus agricultural products, cotton, rubber and the like? In the discussions in the United States Senate there has been a tremendous change in the viewpoint of the legislators of that country. The consensus is that the danger of all-out war has greatly diminished in the last year and a half. Apparently that view is shared by the
Supply-National Defence Minister of National Defence, as one reads between the lines. But how are we to meet the challenge of the U.S.S.R.?
Mention was made of the D.E.W. line, a most costly project; but many of those who gave evidence before the United States Senate committee, and they were people in authority, seemed to hold the view strongly that the D.E.W. line is almost obsolete before it is completely constructed. In his speech the other day the minister expressed the view that there was no defence, that Canada was in the line of fire and that there was no immediate defence against a potential atomic air war. Has there been any reassessment by Canada and the other NATO nations of the problem of whether a larger or smaller amount shall be devoted to defence and, if a smaller amount, whether larger amounts shall be allocated to defence in the form of aid to underdeveloped countries and with respect to trade matters, the purpose of which would be to meet the challenge of the U.S.S.R.?
We are left in the dark. We do not know. In order to obtain information we have to read the reports of the United States Senate committee or the House of Representatives committee. Why does the government not permit men with the knowledge that General Simonds has and the former adjutant general and men of that kind, who enjoyed the trust of the government for so long, to come before a committee and place the facts before the Canadian people? Are we receiving value for our expenditures? One does not have to have the knowledge gained by committees to conclude that in too large a measure there has been a wasteful disregard of the requirements of the people as a whole and waste of the moneys collected from the people through taxation.
A committee would permit either a revelation of conditions that should not exist, which conditions were set out in detail by the Leader of the Opposition when he referred to General Simonds' criticism, or, on the other hand, those criticisms would be found to be baseless. Personally I believe that with the removal of immediate potential threat of war it is going to be very difficult to maintain the union of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. It is going to be equally difficult to maintain the willingness to sacrifice on the part of the peoples of free nations unless governments take them fully into their confidence and give them the picture as it is, the assurance that for every dollar that is spent there shall be an equivalent value in defence.
In connection with the economic offensive of the U.S.S.R. I asked a moment ago, what
5322	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence is to be the attitude of Canada? Unsuccessful in breaking down the resistance of the free nations by force of arms, the U.S.S.R. now threatens to achieve that end by economic warfare everywhere in the world. Have the nations of NATO not met within recent days, and have they not redefined the respective proportions that the free nations should spend on defence as such, tanks, guns and the like, and what they should spend for humanitarian purposes? President Eisenhower, one of the architects of the preservation of our freedom in the last war, said just a few days prior to being hospitalized:
Every dollar we put into this kind of thing, if it is intelligently spent, is in my mind in the long run worth any $5 we put Just in sheer defence, because in the long run it is a constructive thing.
How are we going to meet the problem? Are we going to continue to expend amounts for defence such as we have spent in recent years in the face of an apparent change of front on the part of the U.S.S.R. that is equally dangerous to us? What are we doing to maintain good relations between Canada and the United States along the D.E.W. line, while at the same time assuring Canada's sovereignty in those areas where the facilities of the D.E.W. line are being constructed? Has the government given consideration to placing at each and every one of the stations along the D.E.W. line official representatives of Canada who will look after immigration, customs and other phases of civil government? However little they may be used, nonetheless the presence of Canadian officials there will give to these areas a realization that they are indeed under our sovereignty and will remove the danger of incidents that lead to disagreement which will otherwise be invited.
There are but a few questions that I would ask the minister to enlarge upon when he replies for, after reading the speech of the minister from beginning to end, one finds in it nothing to indicate that the government of Canada or the Department of National Defence is making plans to meet the changed world concept of the U.S.S.R. It is still maintaining that only by armed defences can freedom be preserved. That has been so, and it was so from 1945 to 1955. In no way suggesting a reduction in defence as such, I ask the minister whether or not Canada, in keeping with what the United States is now doing and what Britain herself is also laying plans to implement, intends to devote some portion-a percentage-of the amounts that are today being utilized for sheer defence in order to meet the world economic offensive of the U.S.S.R.


Certainly that offensive has paid dividends to the U.S.S.R. in the last year and a half. It has met with a far greater degree of success than its military threat and bluster during the period from 1945 to 1955. Are we to have a static Maginot line type of mind in connection with our defences? Or are we in Canada, as one of the major countries within NATO, to join with the other countries of NATO in meeting this new challenge which is as dangerous to our existence as, and in some ways more dangerous than the military challenge of the early years following the second world war?
These are matters that could be looked into in detail in a committee. These are questions that are exercising the minds of the ordinary men and women of our country who on the other hand from day to day, over the radio and in the press, hear and read propaganda to the effect that the danger of war is passing. If this is so, and if there is a change of front on the part of the U.S.S.R., are we going to meet that challenge? Are we going to realize, before it is too late, that economic war as launched by the U.S.S.R., constitutes a great challenge to our existence and is having an amazing effect in Asia and in Africa? It is deluding many people into believing that for the economic security of the present, they are making a fair exchange in giving up their freedom for generations to come.
I have not dealt with the purely military side of defence. What I have tried to do, Mr. Chairman, is place before the minister something of the world situation that we face today when communism changes its front, when it makes a detour from military activities to economic action but at the same time does not change its destination, which is the destruction of freedom everywhere in the world. I ask the minister when he replies to answer this question. Has the Department of National Defence viewed the change of front on the part of the U.S.S.R., and to what extent does it intend to meet that new challenge which is as dangerous as, if not more dangerous than, the military forces that previously represented the policy of the U.S.S.R. in the achievement of the destruction of freedom?
Then I return to the point from which I started in connection with aid to Israel in the fight she is putting up to assure the preservation of her freedom. Have not the events of the last three months-revealing as they do Nasser in a new light-given added emphasis to the necessity of an early decision being made on the question of the export of fighting aircraft-not aggressive aircraft such as bombers and the like-to Israel so she will be in such a position, if aggression does

come for which she is in no way responsible, that at least we shall be assured that she will be able to maintain a defence, humble as it may be, against superior and threatening forces.

maintopic: NIAGARA LOWER ARCH BRIDGE COMPANY LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I know the hon. member for Prince Albert would not expect me to follow him and speak about the general strategy of our country on the high plane on which he has spoken in the last few minutes. Certainly in the short time now left to the committee one would not venture to raise such a matter even if one possessed the ability so to do. Hence for the few minutes which remain this afternoon, perhaps I might refer to some matters in a more mundane sphere, but ones equally important to the people involved.
I have the honour and the good fortune to represent a constituency which has within it three of the larger defence bases in this country. One of them is H.M.C.S. Cornwallis, which I believe is the largest naval training base in the British commonwealth. Another one is Greenwood, which I am told is the largest operational air base in Canada. Another one is Aldershot, an army base which, although much smaller, has a distinguished record and a great history. The name is associated with Aldershot camp in Britain which so many veterans of the first war as well as of the second war visited and at which they took training while there. Under such circumstances I come in close contact with the men at these bases and also with the civilian employees who are employed in civilian work there.
I certainly join with the minister in all he said on Wednesday with respect to the calibre of the men we have in our armed forces. I think we can be very proud indeed of the type of men who are found in each one of the three services. Of the quality of their training, their character, their morale and all the rest of it, one cannot speak too highly. When it comes to the civilian employees, some question has been raised-and I think questions can be raised-as to the amount of money which is paid for civilian employees in the over-all picture. It seems to be an extremely large amount. In some places I think real criticism could be levelled at that situation. But when it comes to those
working at the lower levels, Mr. Chairman__
the day labourer, so-called, or the hourly-pay man-I think perhaps a word could be said on the other side of the picture.
I have here communications-I am not going to read them all to the committee-from various organizations at both H.M.C.S. Cornwallis and Greenwood. I also have communications from Aldershot, though there
Supply-National Defence the number of men is not nearly so large. I realize that there is difficulty in the administration of this department on the part of the minister. I realize it must work in co-operation with the Department of Labour. The Department of Labour is supposed to make surveys to establish wage rates. Then those wage rates, having been established or having been approved by the Department of Labour, are recommended to the Department of National Defence; the Department of National Defence approves them and finally recommends them to treasury board, and after a long period of months some adjustment may be made. As a result there are many inconsistencies creeping into the picture, and I think some real unfairness.
I have a letter here, but I do not propose to read it. I could give it to the minister if he would like to see it, because in the letter the man tells me that he has cleared this with the civilian labour officer there, who has suggested that the matter be dealt with at a higher level because he cannot deal with it himself. This is a case of an hourly-pay man working at a rate which pays him $39.60 per week. He is in charge of the inspection, maintenance and operation of eight boilers in this base where he is working. The men who are firing the boilers, and really working under him, are civilians getting $51.92 per week. He does not suggest for a moment that they are getting paid too much but it does seem rather strange in this particular case that a man who is actually a technician and has these firemen assist him when he is effecting repairs, gets that take-home pay of $39.60 compared with $51.92 for the others. The others, as he says, get the benefit of sick leave, vacations with pay and so forth, none of which he receives.
In the mail this morning there was a notice from the civil service, which all of us get every day, advertising the same type of position at Gagetown, a mechanic to supervise, repair and maintain furnaces and boilers. The salary is set at $3,150 per year to $3,600. It does seem to me there is an inconsistency there. Apparently this man has tried, the civilian boss has tried, without results. Whenever these men write me I warn them that I dare not use their names because they may get into trouble. Apparently ministers do not like these people writing to politicians, and perhaps rightly so. In this case I have been told I could use his name. That is typical of only one individual.
I have a petition here signed by the electricians complaining that they have been waiting now for a year and a half to have their wages raised. It is true that six months ago they received an increase of 10 cents an hour, but the rates are ridiculously low in

Supply-National Defence comparison with the regular wages being paid electricians, even in that area. At one time the Department of Labour took a very small area, just the valley itself where there were very few tradesmen, mechanics or electricians, so the base was very small. Now it has been extended to some extent and they take some of the other towns within the province. There again, you get this objection from these men who say they have submitted briefs over the last two or three years showing the rates of wages prevailing in the same industry in the same area. Every time something happens. As I said before, we finally succeeded in getting them an increase of 10 cents an hour six months ago, but that does not go very far.
In so far as the day labourers are concerned, the situation is rather grim. I have a resolution, a copy of which I presume was sent to the minister, as the letter says. I shall just read one paragraph from it to show the feelings of some of these men:
We, the labourers of Cornwallis naval base, are 100 per cent veterans.
I think that is a slight exaggeration, because I sometimes get letters from people who are applying for positions there who say they are veterans and they cannot get on but there are non-veterans employed. There is, therefore, at least an element of exaggeration in this first sentence, and I think there may be an exaggeration in the second sentence. This shows the extent of the bitterness that is creeping in.
We are not getting used as human beings. Some of us labourers are renting homes: some are trying to buy their homes. We are married men with families trying to send our children to school. The ones responsible for this know very well that they cannot clothe, feed and keep up a comfortable home for their families on a weekly pay of $32.22-our take home pay.
That is for day labourers, the lowest class of pay at Cornwallis naval base. You get inconsistencies such as that, Mr. Chairman, and the men included in that day labour base are sometimes transferred to work with civil servants. As I said, they do not complain about the pay the civil servant gets, but they do feel that their own rate of pay should be raised.
I think it is time for the minister to take up very seriously with the Department of Labour
the matter of a resurvey of the pay for hourly-paid men, and I presume the women. There are women employed in the canteens; some of them work as domestics, waitresses and so forth in the dining halls at both Cornwallis and Greenwood. This situation is one which causes friction and does not tend to improve the morale in any organization. I think the minister, if he asks for an investigation by the Department of Labour or for reports from his own representatives, might well find that some of these complaints are legitimate and that a slight amelioration of them could be made without any increase in cost.
There are other places where savings could be made. If time permitted I could point them out. I might point out one in the last minute available to me. I have seen bills of lading for kegs of nails which have been shipped 3,000 miles across this country. These ordinary nails have been shipped to a base in Nova Scotia from Alberta, and the freight transportation costs shown in the bill of lading were away beyond what one would have to pay for these nails at a local store in the community. I have a dozen documents of that kind showing that apparently there is a certain degree of inefficiency and a high degree of waste in expenditures such as that.
It is for that reason some of these men who are on prevailing rates are so angry. They see money being wasted on the one hand and they are being paid a pittance on the other. They feel that something should be said on their behalf, and that is what I am trying to do in the few minutes that are available to me.
May I call it six o'clock?
Progress reported.
Could we have the business for Monday?
